speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to bring to the attention of the government certain utterances by the President of the United States, as reported in the press. Speaking at Atlanta, Ga., on the 10th day 157
of March, he is reported to have used these words:
When we entered upon the negotiations I asked the Secretary of State and his commissioners to offer free trade in everything, but this Canada could not grant us, because slie has a protective system and she was afraid of the competition of our better-organized industries.
I would like to ask whether or not this is a correct statement, and I would like to call attention to this further circumstance: We have not, in respect to these negotiations, any information in this House as to offer or counter-offer one way or the other. In that respect the information with regard to these negotiations is very much less than the information which has usually been given to the House when treaties or arrangements of this kind have been brought down. If that is a correct statement of fact the House and the country are entitled to know it, and I think the House and the country are also entitled to know what other oral negotiations in reference to these matters took place. It is not desirable that we should have a one-sided or partial statement. If the President of the United States feels himself at liberty to make this part of the oral negotiations public, I see no reason why all of the oral negotiations should not be disclosed to this House. They would certainly, it seems to me, have been disclosed to this House and the country if they had been conducted in writing. They were not conducted in writing, apparently, but nevertheless they are equally important, and it is equally desirable that we should have the information. I should like also to ask what is the understanding of the government with respect to one further matter. Is Canada, on the one hand, or the United States, on the other, under the terms of this arrangement, at liberty to grant or to continue bounties, or to impose export duties on all or any of the articles and products which are included in the agreement? I mention that because some question has arisen in the discussion before the Committee on Ways and Means in the United States Senate in respect to a matter closely touching that particular point, and I would think it only right that we should have the view of the government with respect to that particular question.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be permitted first to answer the last question that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) put. There is no agreement, understanding or anything of the kind as between the Canadian government and the United States that is not set forth in the documents in the possession of the House. That is my best answer to my hon. friend regarding bounties, countervailing duties, export duties or anything of the sort. The document speaks for



itself. With regard to the other question, my hon. friend quotes from the President of the United States as follows:
When we entered upon these negotiations X ashed the Secretary of State and his commissioners to offer free trade in everything, but this Canada could not grant us, because she has a protective system and she was afraid of the competition of our better-organized industries.
That statement may be entirely correct, and I have no doubt is, as to the instructions that the President gave to his officials. But, as to what actually occurred in the conference, the matter did not advance to a position which would enable these gentlemen to make such a formal offer in that way. At the very earliest stage in the negotiations we certainly gave them to understand that we could not undertake to have any free trade in manufactures, speaking generally. There are certain articles which are on the free list and which were not the subject of discussion, but speaking generally, we gave them to understand that we were not prepared to deal with them on the basis of free trade in manufactures. That circumstance was clearly expressed by us at the beginning and no formal offer such as that suggested was ever made. Yet the statement is no doubt substantially correct as to the willingness of the President of the United States. I do not agree with my hon. friend that the information furnished as to the proceedings of the conference differs in any way from information furnished under similar circumstances at other times.

speechtext: ['But the depositors are the people who are suffering.\nOn motion of Mr. Edwards, debate was adjourned.\nOn motion of Sir Wilfrid Lauxier, House adjourned at 12.07 a.m. Thursday.', 'Thursday, March 16, 1911.']

Mr. Speaker, I propose to bring to your attention a matter which I judge to be of sufficient importance to engage the attention of the House for a short time. I refer to the failure of the Farmers' Bank. This question is one of very deep interest to myself, inasmuch as my constituents, whom I more particularly represent here, are very deeply interested. In the small county of Halton, perhaps one of the smallest counties in Ontario, there was subscribed to the stock of this bank $196,200, involving a liability to these shareholders of $392,400 if the double liability of the shareholders should be exacted. Apart from that, there were deposits in two agencies in the county of $69,581, making a total possible loss- and I say possible loss, because I have at the present time very little hope indeed that much will be saved out of this wreck- of $461,981. In a small county like that hon. gentlemen can readily understand that to the farmers who are most deeply interested, they being chiefly the subscribers to the stock, it will almost mean a panic; in fact, if no redress is obtained the county will be paralysed by this loss. The bank Mr. FIELDING.
was called the Farmers' Bank, a name well chosen to enlist the sympathy of the farmers. The farmers were proud to have a bank taking their own name, and to my mind this was perhaps the strongest reason why these men so largely fell into line and subscribed so liberally to the stock. The farmers, as I said before, were the chief subscribers to this stock. There were others, some business men, some professional men, but chiefly those engaged in agricultural pursuits undertook to float the stock of this institution. Some of those farmers will be able to stand the loss, I have no doubt, but there are many to whom it will mean the loss of the savings of a lifetime, and when the loss falls on old men and old women, who have invested their spare means in this way the matter is one for very serious consideration.
I fear that a mortgage will have to be put on the farm in order to enable them to meet their obligations, and the trouble is that many of these people are t-oo far advanced in years ever to redeem that mortgage. Living in this small county there are four directors who are farmers. One of these was placed on the board only at a late date, and to my mind he could not in any way be held responsible for what brought about the wreck of this bank. The other three were, I believe, directors from the organization of the bank, and these four directors together stand to lose $98,200. The question I wish to discuss is: who is responsible for the trouble that has been brought upon these people. Are the shareholders responsible? No, I look upon them as innocent. They were farmers following their regular pursuits, induced by. I believe, largely the name of ' Farmers' Bank ' to engage in this undertaking. They did it in perfect good faith, they thought the matter was perfectly safe. They nominated the directors of the bank, and I believe also appointed the general manager at a meeting held about the 26th November, 1906, a few days before the certificate was given to put this bank into operation. We must bear in mind that until the certificate was granted these directors had very little power indeed. The provisional directors secured the subscriptions of stock and I believe they paid in to the Attorney Genera! of the Dominion a sum of $250,000 in order to secure this certificate. But beyond that, so far as I know, the directors of the bank had no power to spend any money, and I am not aware that they legally spent any other money, although I believe there was some money paid out, not in accord with the terms of the Bank Act. I say that apart from this $250,000 which was paid into the Minister of Finance for the purpose of securing a certificate to enable this bank to go into operation, I do not think the directors had anything to do in the way of expending money. They could do

no business, they could not- borrow, they could not lend in the name of the bank, and consequently the shareholders up to this time felt a great deal of security in as much as no certificate had yet been granted to do business. All the power they had, to my mind, was to complete the organization up to that date. Without the certificate the shareholders money would have been intact; every dollar they had paid in would to-day have been there because the directors had no power to pay it out. The $250,000 paid into the Receiver General would have been intact had the bank gone into operation and be perfectly safe in the hands of the Minister of Finance and could have been returned and paid back to those who subscribed the money, and thus no loss would have accrued. No branch bank could have been opened until authority was given by the Treasury Board to start business; there would have been no liability to depositors, and that is one of the serious matters connected with the whole affair, namely, that the depositors innocently believing the bank was organized on a sound basis came forward readily and placed their money on deposit in the various branches that were opened throughout the country. Only two of these were in the county of Halton, but I think there must have been some 20 or 30 throughout the province, and the sum of $1,281,774 was deposited. Had the certificate never been granted by the Treasury Board the bank could not have gone into operation. There could have been no such thing as the deal in connection with the Keeley mine, which was one of the unfortunate circumstances which brought the bank to ruin and neither could there have been a Trust Company deal, and T do not look upon that with very much favour. Had the certificate not been issued there would have been no bad debts, there would have been no double liability for the shareholders to meet, and to-day the shareholders would have been in a comparatively happy position.

If the hon. gentleman will bear with me for a few momenta I will be very happy to tell him. I said that this $250,000 must be paid out of cash actually paid on stock. If my hon friend _ reads the Bank Act he will find there is no doubt about that, and it was the duty of the Treasury Board to ascertain that that was an actual fact. If the Treasury Board did not do so they failed in their duty because that was one of the things it was necessary for them to know before they could issue a treasury board certificate and launch this bank on the country. I have perused the minutes of the annua] -meeting of the bank and the minutes of the directors' meeting in the early stages of the bank's history, and I have failed to ascertain that either the shareholders or the directors gave any man authority to ask the Treasury Board for a certificate, and I think the authority should have come from that direction. The man who asked the Treasury Board for certificate was the man who had been appointed as managing director. On the 27th of November, Mr. Travers as general manager, by a letter written from Toronto, applied to the Minister of Finance for a certificate to enable him to proceed to open the bank and to d-o an ordinary banking business. That letter was nodoubt received by the Minister of Finance on the 28th of November, and on the 30th of November the Treasury Board granted the certificate. Evidently very little trouble or time was taken to find out the bona fides of the whole matter, and whether this money was really the money of the stockholders or from what source it came. Now, the certificate granted to Mr. Travers enabJed him to do practically as he pleased with the funds of the bank; it enabled him to play ducks and drakes with all the money which the shareholders had paid to him. Only one day intervened between the receipt of the requisition and the granting of the certificate. I think one day was too short. I do not hesitate to say that this man, when he asked for the certificate, misled the Minister of Finance.
I would not think anything else. I am quite sure the representations he made were not correct; they are practically admitted to be untrue, and there is no doubt that the Treasury Board, the Minister of Finance particularly, were to a certain extent

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
misled by this representation. I do not think the Treasury Board took the time that was necessary to see whether everything that was put before them was absolutely right, or whether they were justified at all in granting the certificate. The affidavit made by Mr. Travers was submitted to the Deputy Minister o! Justice for his opinion as to whether that was sufficient authority for the Treasury Board to grant a certificate, and I want to draw the attention of hon. members to a very significant [DOT]expression in the answer of the Deputy Minister, a shrewd lawyer who could see through the matter as quickly as any one. j He said that the statements of Mr. Travers were sufficient on which the board could exercise their power of granting a certificate ' if they are accepted.' These four significant words in the letter of the Deputy Minister of Justice to my mind were a warning to the Treasury Board to be careful. He apparently did not think that the statements made by the general manager were reliable or acceptable. Now, there is no doubt that there had not been sufficient money paid in to the provisional directors on account of stock to make up the $250,000. I presume that a great many hon. members have read the proceedings of the curator 'and the liquidator in Toronto, and it is perfectly clear that no such sum of money was available to pay to the Receiver General to obtain this certificate. I contend that in the granting of this certificate there was a direct violation of the Bank Act. That Act is most explicit that every dollar of this $250,000 should be paid in on account of stock, should not. 'be borrowed money or money derived from any other source; and that not having been done in this case was a clear evasion of the Bank Act, and the Treasury Board should have *inquired into the facts. I have before me a copy of the 'Monetary Times,' a journal printed in Toronto that devotes attention to matters of finance, and it deals with this question in a better way than I could; so I am going to read from it a few words to show how the government, or those acting for the government in this matter, were warned. The 'Monetary Times' says:
The day on which the Danners Bank obtained its charter was the first day of Farm-[DOT]ers' Bank deceit. The 'Monetary Times' admits that the government was placed in a delicate position. It could not have gone to Mr. Travers, saying that dishonesty was ram-pant in his institution, and notifying its indention to withdraw the charter. But the -department had six different warnings at various periods of the bank's existence. On October 8, 1906, about a month and a half "before the certificate was granted, Mr. Leighton McCarthy wrote to Mr. Fielding that a number of subscribers to the shares of the *Farmers' Bank would dispute the bona fide Mr. HENDERSON
character of the subscriptions. 'Grave conditions have arisen,' he said, 'which require careful consideration before the Treasury Board grant any certificate to the organizing of this bank.' In a subsequent letter dated October 19, Mr. McCarthy again wrote the Minister of Finance formally asking that the Treasury Board stay any action on the application of the Farmers' Bank for a certificate.
Now, 1 may be told that later on Mr. McCarthy withdrew his protest, assigning as a reason that his clients had been settled with by the bank, and therefore he had no further claim to make, but even supposing that his clients had been setT tied with the fact remains that the government had information that there was something decidedly wrong.
Mr. Fielding wrote to Mr. Travers, stating that in a previous case there had been an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act, and that subscribers to stock had given their note instead of paying in cash. Mr. Travers replied, 'I have to say that in the case of the Farmers' Bank of Canada the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way maintained by you.'
The information was that the provisional directors or Mr. Travers had raised this money, or a considerable portion of it, by taking the notes of shareholders who had paid for only a part of their stock, discounting these notes in the bank or in a trust company, and using the proceeds for the purpose of making up what was required of the $250,000, after exhausting the money they had from such stock subscriptions. Now there were two occasions on which the attention of the government was drawn forcibly to this very circumstance which Mr. McCarthy complained of, because the trouble with Mr. McCarthy's clients was that they had given notes for part of their stock and discovered afterwards that their notes had been endorsed by the provisional directors and discounted in other banks for the purpose of raising money to meet the deposit necessary to secure a certificate, which was clearly an evasion of the banking law.	.
I am now going to mention mother circumstance, which, I think, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will quite well remember. As I told you, Mr. Speaker, I felt a very deep interest in the affairs of this bank owing to the fact that so much money was at stake in it from the county I have the honour to represent. I felt very much worried not because of any personal interest for I had refused to subscribe to any of the stock, although asked to do so. I refused because I had not sufficient faith in the concern to warrant my doing so-. It was not, therefore, for any personal reason that I felt so much interested but simply because I had a deep regard for the wel-

fare of the men in' my county who had pledged their credit, ranging from $100 up to as high as $22,000, which, with the double liability, would mean a liability of from $200 to $44,000. I went therefore to the Minister of Finance myself and spoke to him about this. I told him that I felt very uncomfortable over Ithe matter and was afraid there was going to be trouble.
Was that before the certificate was granted?

Yes, and I told him the reason why I was anxious. That the reason was that very many of my constituents were deeply involved in the matter.
I said to him:	I have personal knowledge of this because I have seen notes in the hands of the solicitor who was acting for some ten or a dozen of these men, and who had taken proceedings against the bank and had forced it to give back the money they had paid and the notes they had signed. He had forced the bank to do this because the provisional directors were not carrying out the spirit and intent of the Bank Act. I had seen those notes. They were endorsed by the provisional directors for the purpose of raising money, presumably to provide the necessary deposit of $250,000 to get the certificate and enable the bank to begin business. Let me now read the answer given by the Minister of Finance to a question asked by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and I consider that 1 am justified in mentioning these facts [DOT]because of the position I occupy in this House as representing these men. Under the 30th January last the hon. member for North Toronto asked this question:
Did the Finance Department, or any of its officials, the Finance Minister or any other member of the government, receive any communication, verbal or written, previous to the issue of the certificate of the Treasury Board to the Farmers' Bank, cautioning, warning or suggesting an inquiry as to the standing or character of the promoters, or the proceedings by which the deposit was procured.
The hon. minister replied as follows:
The government did not receive in any form any information which afforded ground for a refusal of the deposit.
The hon. member for North Toronto was not satisfied with that answer, and later on in the day repeated his question and pointed out that the answer given was not really a reply to the question he had put. He said:
I beg leave to point out to the House that the answer given is not an answer to my question. I think I have a right to an answer to my question, then the House, as well as myself would form its own opinion as to whether it afforded ground for any interference.
To this the Finance Minister replied:
There was some gossip in banking circles concerning the Farmers' Bank, of which we became aware. I do not see how we can take cognizance of that. There is an answer as to any representation that was made in the proper way. There was gossip abroad concerning the Farmers' Bank, I was welt artare of it.
I presume that the hon. minister intended to include me among those who were retailing gossip.
M(r. FIELDING. I can relieve my hon. friend's mind on that point. I had no such intention.

I am very glad indeed to have that statement because I can assure the hon. minister that I had no intention of retailing gossip. I went to him with a straight fact that came under my personal knowledge, and I felt it mv duty, as representing a county in which large amounts of money were at stake in this concern, to make the representation that I did. The Minister of Finance treated me with the greatest courtesy. He told me that he would hold the certificate back as long as he could. That certainly is evidence that my representation to him was made before the certificate was granted.

The hon. gentleman says that he was uneasy and anxious because people in his riding had invested in the stock of that bank. Would he say definitely what information he gave to the minister and whether he asked the minister to withhold the certificate.

I think I made my statement sufficiently clear. I shall Tepeat again so that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) may understand it. I told him I was deeply interested in the matter of the Farmers' Bank foT the reason that a very-large amount of money, practically almost half the stock of the bank was subscribed in my county. I realized at this time that it might create a panic in the county if the worst came to the worst, and the bank should fail and the double liability be exacted. I told him that I myself, had seen promissory notes made by farmers in my county, endorsed by the provisional directors that had been used, as I was informed and verily believed for the purpose of raising money presumably to make up the $250,000 required in order to get a certificate. No other money was wanted by the provisional directors. They did not require to borrow money foT any other purpose; they had no authority to borrow money at all, and this borrowing wa= altogether improper. Now, I made that statement, and I thought that was a warning to the Minister of Finance to beware of the men with whom he wat

dealing, and that he should be on his guard. The Minister of Finance accepted my statement in that light, and, as I said, with all the courtesy that was required, he told me that he would hold the certificate back as long as he could. I confess that I left the Minister of Finance feeling quite safe. I thought the matter was in the strong hands of a strong man, who stood between the subscribers to this stock and the government, a man^who was in a position to defend my constituents and prevent them being defrauded. Shortly afterward, the minister met me in the corridor-there was no secrecy about this conversation, never so^ intended by me, or I believe, by the minister-and informed me that Mr. Travers had been down, and that he had brought his money. And the minister said - (I will use his own words)-' I put it up to him and he denied it.' What was it the minister ' put up to him?' What did the minister wish me to understand he had put up to him,' but the very statement I had made to him a short time before? And Mr. Travers denied it. He then asked Mr. Travers to give him a letter to that effect, declaring that my statement was untrue. And he accepted that letter and gave Mr. Travers this certificate. He believed Mr. Travers whom he had never met, perhaps, until a few days before-because I believe he was introduced to him by Mr. Calvert,-he accepted Travers' wordsj and repudiated mine, although I had sat in the House with him for fifteen years and we had always been on the best of terms. I confess that, when I heard the minister say, in answer to a question in this House that ' certain gossip ' had come to him, I felt somewhat hurt; and I am delighted today to heaT the minister say that in using these words he had no reference to myself, and I candidly believe he had not.
Now, I may as well follow this matter to the end In fact, I am compelled to do so, because my constituents think I ought to have something done, something to prevent this terrible holocaust. I met the minister, possibly about two years ago, and he confessed to me that he had some alarm about the Farmers' Bank and related to me the circumstance-which had not then come to my knowledge-that the bank had been peddling in the city of New York a deposit receipt for $150,000 and could not find a purchaser. I confess this looked very suspicious as to the standing of the bank. Before the close of last session, I called on the minister and drew his attention to a matter that had come to my knowledge through a gentleman in Toronto

the clippings of the correspondence that took place in reference to the matter that came up in Syracuse, the purchase of some insurance company. I again repeated to Hr. HENDERSON.
the minister my anxiety over the standing of this bank; for I confess I was anxious, I was worried; not on my own account, but for those who lived in my county, many of whom I knew personally, and for whom I had the greatest respect. And f wish to say in passing, that I am not speaking particularly on behalf of my political friends, because the men who stand to lose the most money in that county are men who are the political friends of hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. I make no point of that, but I do not wish it to be understood that I interested myself in this matter along political lines. As I say, I called on the minister and told him that, owing to the correspondence that appeared in the paper, I thought there was danger to the Farmers' Bank. The minister was familiar with what had taken place, and, seeing that I was somewhat worried over the matter, he very kindly said to me, ' Henderson, I 'don't see why you should worry over this; you are not responsible; besides, you did warn the government.' Those were the explicit words of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am bound to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) that I shall have to take exception to that statement later on.

I make that statement of my own knowledge, from distinct recollection;-and you can understand, Sir, and I think the House will understand, how vividly it was impressed upon my mind from what I have said of the anxiety I had concerning the standing of this bank. The minister says he will have to take exception to my statement, but I must ask him, as one member of this House, as one has a right to ask another, to accept this statement, I will not put it in the extreme form, but I adhere to it; the statement I made is absolutely correct.
So much, then, for the reason why the Treasury Board should have been on their guard, and should have refused the certificate at the time. The government unfortunately, did not heed the warning. Had they delayed and investigated, I am hopeful that, they would have disovered that this man was not entitled to the certificate to open this bank; and I repeat, if no certificate had been issued, this unfortunate affair would have been avoided.
Now, we ask the question:	Who is responsible?-for I look upon this as the crux of the whole matter. I may be told that the officers of the bank named by the shareholders are responsible. I cannot agree to that proposition, because as I have already stated, the officers named by the bank had no power to squander the money of the bank. All the money they could pay out legally was the $250,000. ' That they

had the right to do and did, I think, about the 23rd of October prior to the issue of the certificate. So, I fail to see that the shareholders are responsible in any way because their officers were guilty of wrongdoing. The Bank Act, in fact, delegates to the government, the power to safeguard the shareholders. That is the business of the government. Why was the clause put in the Bank Act forbidding the issuing of a certificate until all the formalities had been complied with? That was certainly to safeguard the public, those who had put their money into the institution, and one of the matters that I refer to more especially is the fact that the money that was sent down here to make the deposit was only in part the money derived from the sale of stock. Those who have been following the reports of the curator or liquidator in Toronto will have ascertained that only $170,000 of the shareholders' money was available for that purpose, and that there was borrowed from another institution $80,000 to make up the $250,000. I assume that if the evidence came out, that money was paid back to that institution which advanced the $80,000 after the $245,000 had been returned by the Receiver General to the bank in Toronto.
Now I contend that the most rigid inquiry ought to be made into this whole matter. 1 do not think that a liquidator in Toronto, or the curator who is dealing with that matter, has the power to deal with it, as it ought to be dealt with. What right have they to come down here and investigate the doings of this government? To the actions of this government, or to those on the Treasury Board, I think we must look for the origin of the trouble, and for the cause of the calamity. Therefore, I say we must pursue some other course, and my suggestion is that a full and thorough inquiry by a Royal Commission alone could bring out the information that is desired. If the shareholders alone are responsible through the men thaiPThew aiyphtnled, I qquld noT argJ5~hTrrThat they' wouldTiave tQjsuBerTEeToss alone,~tEey~wou]dTiave to suffeT~ahy loss if-they alone were responsible. But if these officers did not do anything that could dissipate their money, if they were not alone responsible, then I believe that we must look further; and if the government of this country was misled or deceived, or through lack of care in any way neglected to investigate the matter before a certificate was given to launch this bank, before giving the general manager power, as I said before, to play ducks and drakes with what was left of the shareholders' money, then I think that not the shareholders, but this country ought to come to the rescue for any loss that has been made. I submit that this country is big enough, rich enough and generous
enough to maintain its honour, and I do not see how the honour of this government or of this country could be maintained in this matter unless they came down with something to assist these poor people, and help them out of the difficulty which they have unfortunately fallen into. To do that requires an inquiry over and above anything that could be brought out under the Winding Up Act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move:
That all the words after the word 'that' in (he proposed motion be omitted and the following substituted therefor:
This House is of opinion that a Royal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate the incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, and the granting of a certificate by the Treasury Board permitting said bank to issue notes and transact business, and all the circumstances connected therewith; and generally to inquire into and investigate the operation and efficiency of the Bank Act in relation to the affairs and transactions of said bank.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance*).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With that portion of my hon. friend's remarks which deals with the misfortunes that have fallen upon these good citizens of Canada, and upon other good citizens of Canada, I am sure we all deeply sympathize. But though we may deeply sympathize with these good citizens in the misfortunes which have come upon them, it does not follow that we would be justified in treating them differently from all other citizens who have the misfortune to make an unhappy investment. A short time ago my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) put a question on the Order Paper, and an answer was given on behalf of the government. I propose to read the question and the answer, because in a very short form they present the case on both sides:

What action does the government intend to take on tlie two requests preferred by the deputation on behalf of tlie shareholders and depositors of the Farmers' Bank, viz., that a Royal Commission be appointed to make a thorough examination into all matters connected with the incorporation and management of the Farmers' Bank; and that legislation be enacted to relieve shareholders of their double liability and to enable depositors to be paid at least fifty cents on the dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The government have no reason to doubt that the exercise of the powers given to the liquidator by law, and the performance of the duties imposed upon that officer by like authority, and the proceedings now engaging the attention of the courts of justice in Toronto, will, lead to a full investigation into and disclosure of all the affairs of the bank, and that, therefore, there is no need of the appointment of a Royal Commission. Should anything arise later to indicate that the investigation is insufficient, the question can be further considered. Re-

530S
plying to the latter part of the hon. gentleman's question, the government deeply regret that a number of people who are not well able to bear the loss are likely to suffer from the failure of the bank, but in the judgment of the government it would be contrary to public policy to recoup the losses of any class of investors from the public treasury.
There has been no change in the condition of affairs since that answer was given. An investigation has been undertaken in part by the curator, and subsequently in part by the liquidator, the machinery of the courts has been invoked, and has been occupying a great deal of attention of the courts in the province of Ontario, and I see no reason to doubt that the investigation will be thorough. With regard to the investigation of the circumstances connected with the issue of the certificates, all that is a matter of record which is before the House. No investigation would bring forth anything material that is not now in the possession of the House, or is not within easy reach of the House. Therefore, we are unable to see that the situation is in any respect changed, or that there is any need of a Royal Commission to investigate matters which are already being fully investigated in the courts.
There are three stages in the proceedings in connection with the Farmers' Bank. There is, first, the incorporation of the bank; second, the issue of the certificate; third, the operations of the bank after organization. I desire to invite the attention of the House to each of these stages separately. My hon. friend, in his address, made no reference whatever to the incorporation although I see that in his motion he has included the incorporation of the bank as one of the matters which might require investigation
I certainly understood the issue of the certificate to be part of the incorporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad in that respect that my hon. friend has mentioned it, because he did not mention it in his remarks. But, inasmuch as the incorporation of this bank has been the subject of very much discussion outside, it is as well that in considering the matter, we should give some attention to the circumstances under which the Act of incorporation was obtained. We have a general Act governing banking operations, but each bank has its individual and separate charter. Each bank comes to this House with a private Bill for the purpose of obtaining incorporation. It is not a matter particularly of government concern. Any individual member has the right, and exercises the right, of bringing in a Bill to provide for the incorporation of a new bank. The matter is usually investigated by the Commit-Mr. FIELDING.
tee on Banking and Commerce. In that committee the government have no particular rights. A member of the government at the committee has precisely the same-right as all. other members have. While the government will naturally feel an interest in all legislation, I am one of those who think that in the matter of private legislation, it is not well that the government should at all times project itself into the discussion and endeavour to have these matters take a party turn. So, in private legislation there is always very great freedom claimed by an individual member, which is not always the case with regard to general legislation initiated by the government or perhaps by hon. gentlemen opposite. The government, of course, have an interest in all legislation, and in that sense are responsible for legislation generally, but it is a fact that the method of dealing with private Bills differs somewhat from the manner in which general legislation is handled.
This bank was incorporated in 1904. I do not remember that any exception was taken to the incorporation at thait time. The bank was not organized at that time. The promoters came back in 1905 for an extension and received it. In the year 1906 they came back again. Now, as I said a moment ago, that committee is composed of gentlemen from both sides of the House, and if there had been any objection to the incorporation of the bank, it would have been well that we should have heard it and that those who opposed it should have placed themselves on record. As far as my memory goes, the only objection that was ever raised to the incorporation of this bank, came from myself and from some members who may later on, have shared my view. But, to the original incorporation, I do not remember that any objection wras taken. We have to consider a moment the general principles governing bank incorporation. The business of Canada has been increasing faster than the available banking capital. It is desirable that we should have from time to time additional banking capital. Whether that should be obtained by increasing the capital of existing banks or by the creation of new banks, is not, perhaps, a matter of great concern, but that the country with its rapid growth should have further capital *will be generally admitted. Whenever a proposition is made to incorporate a new bank, the committee is rather disposed to view it in a friendly light. I do not know whether there was any objection taken to the incorporation in 1904 nor can I recall anything in particular with regard to the application which was made in 1905. In 1906 the promoters came back again and I then opposed the granting of a charter. My view was that the fact that they had not

been able to organize promptly, indicated that they were having difficulty, and I confess that from the beginning I did not quite like the name of the Farmers' Bank. My fear was, that possibly the granting of the charter in 1905 would have the effect of inducing people to engage in the banking business, who were not likely to realize the responsibility they were assuming in becoming shareholders. However, the sentiments of members differed as they sometimes do in the Banking and Commerce Committee. Some hon. gentlemen were not in harmony with my own view and after some discussion, I found I could not carry niy views as to the rejection of the charter, but, it was agreed that they should at all events, be permitted a six months extension and I think I probably assented to that. At all events, I know that I succeeded in obtaining a reduction of the period for which the extension was granted. If it had not been granted what would have been said? At the time this argument was put to me, members friendly to the venture came and said: You must not oppose this charter, Mr. Minister. The country needs banking capital and there is a good deal of feeling in the country that the old banks have a monopoly of the business. I do not quite endorse that, but there is a good deal of that feeling, and these gentlemen said: If you are going to oppose the efforts of the farmers to have a share in the banking business of the country, you will be met with the cry that parliament is giving the eld banks a monopoly, and is not willing to give a fair chance to the farmers. In the Banking and Commerce Committee that feeling leads us to grant charters sometimes when possibly some of us would prefer that they should not grant them. At all events under these [DOT] circumstances and with that feeling on my part, the charters was granted by this parliament after it had been reported by the Banking and Commerce Committee of which many hon. gentlemen opposite are members and for which I take whatever share of responsibility I have as a member of that committee. Therefore, I think I can say at once that in so far as the granting of the charter is concerned, there is no room now for any complaint against the action of this government, or for that matter, against the action of this parliament. I am taking my responsibility as one member of this committee and of this parliament. Although I would have preferred that the charter should not continue to exist I accepted the compromise of a six months extension, and of course, I accept responsibility for that with my colleagues on the committee. Therefore, I say that parliament is responsible for the granting
of the charter and I do not think that any reasonable ground of objection can be taken to the incorporation of the new bank in face of the fact that the incorporation of new banks is still regarded as generally desirable.
Now, we come to the second question, the granting of the certificate. I want to say in, that connection that my chief regret is that I have to have a difference of opinion _ with my respected friend from Halton. I know him too well to hesitate for a moment in accepting any statement that he might make. I credit him with all good faith and sincerity, and if he and I do not agree as to what has occurred that does not imply that I for one moment question the good faith or veracity of my hon. friend, but it simply means that I am obliged to say that, my hon. friend is mistaken. I am obliged to say when my hon. friend tells me that he warned me against the issue of this certificate that he is mistaken. My hon. friend and I have had frequent conversations over the question of this bank. I do not recall, however, that we met in any formal way, but we met at different times as members-of the House do, and we had conversations-concerning the bank. That arose from the fact that my hon. friend knew I was opposed to the granting of the charter and that I viewed it with anxiety. The conversations-between my hon. friend and myself were always along the line that we regretted the necessity for the creation of this Farmers' Bank, we were sorry to have the farmers of the country engaging in banking when, in the case of many of them, they were not familiar with the responsibilities which would be involved in the acceptance of shares of a bank. All our conversations were along that line. We were feeling sorry that the farmers were going into this matter, but I can assure my hon. friend that when he says that he warned me against the issue of the certificate, although I know he makes the statement in all good faith,
I am bound to say that to the best of my recollection he is entirely mistaken. Nothing of the kind occurred.
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) wish that denial to apply to the three interviews at which there were conversations or only to the last one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember how many conversations I had with my hon. friend.
There were three that were mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No matter how many-there were, in so far as they took place before the issue of the certificate, I mean my denial to apply to all. I had conversations with my hon. friend from time to time-as to the regret which we both had about I the farmers going into this bank, but I dis-

tinctly state that my hon. friend is wrong when he says that he warned me against the issue of a certificate. He says that I decided to accept the statement of Mr. Travers as against him.
I am bound to say that if the matter ever did take that shape-with my hon. friend a wfitness on one side-knowing my hon. friend for many years as well as I do -and having on the other side a gentleman who I did not know at all, I would unhesitatingly accept my hon. friend's statement. But I wish to say that the matter never did take that position at all; there never was any conflict with my hon. friend on one side and Manager Travers on the other. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) says that I told him-he is very clear about it, and he presumes to quote the exact language- that I Cput it up' to him (Mr. Travers). Well, if I were not sure otherwise I would certainly be sure from that, because I do not believe that I ever used such a phrase in my life. Whatever faults I have in the elegance of my language, I am quite satisfied that I never used such an expression, and therefore I can say my hon. friend does not recollect that correctly. However, that is not very important.
I must say that my recollection of that is very distinct, and I think that the minister ought to accept my word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must remember that I am no more bound to accept his word than he is to accept mine.
I made my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I make my statement.
You have no right to contradict my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nor has my hon. friend any right to contradict mine.
I am not contradicting yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we need have no conflict over that. I say at once that I have too much regard for my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to suggest for a single moment that he would make any statement in this House that he did not make in all sincerity, and believe to be absolutely correct. I would do my hon. friend and myself an injustice if I suggested anything of the sort; but I am bound to say that his memory is wrong as to what occurred.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
While my hon. friend and I had occasional conversations about the affairs of this bank they all arose out of the fact that I had opposed the granting Mr. FIELDING
of this charter and viewed the matter with some anxiety.

I must take exception to that statement. I have no recollection of ever discussing with him the impropriety of granting these people a charter. I was on the Banking and Commerce Committee and supported the granting of that charter which was originally, I think, in the hands of the hon. member for South Wellington, and I representing farmers of Canada never objected to them getting a charter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that my hon. friend objected to giving the charter. I said I had objected to giving the charter, and as hon. members who sat with me on the committee are aware I reluctantly agreed to give them a six-months' extension, and it was out of that discussion arising in that way that my hon. friend and I occasionally had conversation. Certain portions of the conversation he has repeated and certain others he has not, but that is not material. I must say frankly that while I am not complaining of his repeating the conversations, and while I would not think myself free to repeat them under the circumstances, I do not complain. I said nothing to my hon. friend that might not be said from the house tops.

Does the hon. gentleman consider that the conversation on a public matter o'f that kind was private? I certainly never considered it so. When I make representations concerning a public matter of interest to my constituents I would consider that they are perfectly open.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not complaining; I said that I did not consider myself free to repeat the conversation I had with my hon. friend, but my hon. friend has a different view as to that. Might I ask the hon. gentleman how it is, if it was a grave and serious matter affecting his constituents as he now says, he did not take the trouble to put his views in writing so that they might go on record and be beyond dispute) If my hon. friend felt as keenly in the matter as he now does, if he believed that the granting of this certificate was about to coime to pass, and if he had good reasons against it, surely my hon. friend would be bound by his duties to his constituents to have addressed me a letter and have his views on record, and then there would be no room for dispute.

While I believed there was trouble I was extremely anxious not to say anything more than -was absolutely necessary in case that might bring about the collapse of an institution which eventually might work its way through. I considered that mv personal verbal statement to the minister which was intended for him as a warning was just as good as

if I had put it in writing, and I stated the reason why I preferred that mode rather than putting a document on file which might have been read by others and construed into an attempt on my part to wreck a bank which might otherwise pull through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that that remark might apply very well after the bank was organized, but it does not apply to a time when the bank was not organized at all, and when there was no bank to wreck. He says it is before the certificate was granted he warned me against it, and if so there is no reason why that warning should not be put in writing. Did my hon. friend then attach the same importance to it that he does now he should have done himself the justice of putting that warning in writing.
I did not regard it at the time as a necessity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a rule public business is transacted in writing; as a rule when men wish to bring about important transactions they exchange letters which will make the matter clear and place it beyond the possibility of any dispute, and if the hon. gentleman fails to do that and leaves it to a matter of memory, well, his memory is just as likely to be treacherous as that of any other hon. gentleman. I want to say distinctly that the conversation my hon. friend and I had, had no reference to any warning and that I never received from him any warning as to the issue of the certificate to this bank.
Is not the minister's memory likely to be treacherous on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is possible. I am admitting that my hon. friend from Halton makes the statement in absolute sincerity, but I say that my recollection is that he is wrong. If he wishes to think that my recollection is wrong and his is right we will have to leave it at that. The fact that he failed to put it in writing is rather a misfortune in view of the difference of opinion that has arisen.

I would tell the Minister of Finance that I have ere this put my views in writing and a minister of the government of which he was a member, although these views were marked ' private,' published them in a blue-book and sent them broadcast all over the country to try and do me an injury. I do not mean to say that the minister of finance would have published this in order to do me an injury. I am quite satisfied he would not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How could I have done mv hon. friend an injury?
It might be insinuated that I made an attempt to wreck the bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would stand now to my hon. friend's infinite credit if he had warned me and iE I had gone on despite the warning. However, my hon. friend did not take that course, and I will leave that matter as it is. The first stage in this matter of the issue of the certificate is to be found in a communication from Mr. Leighton McCarthy, who says he is instructed by some shareholders, his clients, to object to the issue of the certificate, and he states in a subsequent letter that he complains that in some cases where large sums of money have been paid, notes have also been given. Now, at that time the application for a certificate had not yet been received. Mr. McCarthy was informed there was no application, and that when the application did come his representation would have all due consideration. Mr. McCarthy's letters on that subject were dated October 8th and 19th. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) has spoken of very great haste on this question, and he has said that the application for the certificate was written on the 27th, presumably received on the 28th, and the certificate was granted on the 30th November; but if my hon. friend will look through the correspondence he will see that on the 23rd of October Mr. Travers took the first step toward the organization by depositing the $250,000 in the Bank of Montreal, and notify ing the department that he deposited it for the purpose of organizing the bank. So mv hon. friend will see that we had notice of the application and the money in our possession for some considerable time before the dates he has mentioned.
May I ask the hon. minister if he had any letters warning him as to this bank other than that of Mr. Leighton McCarthy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I am Tight in saying that there were no other letters. The day after the certificate was granted, a letter came from the Canadian Bankers' Association.
As a matter of fact, did not a local manager write to you warning you of this bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Any letter written to us by a local manager had no reference to the issue of the certificate at all. I think I know what my hon. friend_ refers to. It had reference to another matter later. Mr McCarthy filed his objections, and on the 2nd of November Mr. McCarthy withdrew his objections in a letter in which he says:
Referring to my letters of the 8tli and 9th inst., with referenece to the application for a certificate made on behalf of the Farmers' Bank, I am advised by those who are instructing me that the claims made by them in the action brought have been settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties

interested in the hank and refunding the money paid hy the individuals or returning the notes which had been given. The, objections which I made on their behalf to the issue of the certificates are, therefore, withdrawn. Would you mind therefore returning to me the papers which I forwarded to you?
The papers were, accordingly, returned to Mr. McCarthy. The next stage of the matter was that, anticipating the application, the Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Eoville, wrote to Mr. Travers that it would be desirable that he should furnish a detailed statement of the actual amount of cash paid up in the case of each shareholder. Mr. Travers, in his affidavit, to which I will come in a moment, gave the most positive assurance that the amounts set forth, had been paid in cash. After the declaration of Mr. Travers had been received, although it was in proper order, I thought it desirable that I should see him on the subject. Mr. Travers came to the department in connection with the certificate, and I had a conversation with him, arising out of this note business. At that time-to the best of my knowledge and belief, the only time in my life that I met Mr. Travers,-I had a conversation with him, in which. I called his attention to the fact that there were rumours in banking circles that sometimes the organization of banks was brought about by the use of notes instead of cash. Mr. Travers in the most positive terms declared that there was no foundation for any suspicion of that kind in the present case.
What made you suspicious of Mr. Travers at that particular time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The letter itself says that I had heard of rumours in banking circles that in the case of previous organizations of banks the Bank Act had been evaded by the use of notes. I called Mr. Travers' attention to that and cross-examined him as well as I could on that aspect of the_ question. He assured me in the most positive terms that the cash was paid in, in every case. I think I had dictated a letter to Mr. Travers that was on its way to him, and I said I would like him to give me a written answer, which he did. So that we had before us at the moment of issuing the certificate Mr. Travers' affidavit and Mr. Travers' letter. Now, before we proceed to quote the statements of Mr. Travers, let us reflect for a moment on his present position and on the position he occupied at the time these events occurred. Mr. Travers is now a convict in prison, a discredited man. When you talk of the testimony of Mr. Travers to-day, you evidently think of him as a convict, the prisoner the discredited man. But do not for-Mr. FIELDING
get that at the moment Mr. Travers came before the Department of Finance, he was a man in as good standing as any member of this House, as far as I know. Dear Sir,-I regret that owing to pressing engagements yesterday, arising out of the budget, I was unable to meet you to consider your application for the issue of a certificate to authorize the Farmers' Bank of Canada to commence business. I shall be glad to see you to-day, at my office, at any time before one o'clock if you can call. Or I might be able to see you later, between four and five, at the House of Commons, if that will be more convenient.
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to us that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which has reached us in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to us. I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers' Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.

point to be borne in mind, that, although there was that irregularity-irregularity is too mild a term-although there was that fraud in connection with the payment of the capital at the beginning, although the notes were given when cash should have been given, and all that was wrong and fraudulent; nevertheless, in most cases those notes were ultimately paid, and the cash went into the bank, and the bank did possess the capital at a later stage, though it did not possess it at that moment. The House is responsible and not the government, and every member must take his share of that responsibility. So that, it boots nothing for either of us in this investigation we are carrying on as to the incorporation of the bank. That is a nonessential point in my mind. We cannot fairly _ attribute any fault to the government in the matter and I do not attribute any fault to myself or to other members of the House in that respect. On what ground could you refuse a charter to those who asked for the incorporation of the Farmers bank? You could refuse it onlv; it 1681
seems to me, on the grounds that we had either enough or too many banking institutions in this country already and therefore. there was no room for another. If that approved itself to the committee and the House it would have been fab-ground for refusing the charter. Or, we might have refused the charter because of the personnel of those asking for the charter; if we did not think they had a standing, financial or otherwise, which would give fair belief that they would carry to a successful conclusion the important operation of a banking institution in this country. If these two things were not proven in the negative then the parliament had no right, and the committee had no right, to refuse this bank its incorporation charter, and still less had it ground for refusing it because it was called a farmers' bank. That would have been, to my mind, a reason why the Act of incorporation should have been granted if all other things were equal, and the conditions were complied with; so that we may drop that feature of it out of our consideration. Now, when a bank is incorporated under the Bank Act, it is absolutely innocuous until it is allowed to go into operation. When it is allowed to go into operation it may be a medium of .great benefit and it may be a medium of equally great harm and damage and wrong. The important part of this discussion is, what was the part enacted by the gentlemen in whose charge the Bank Act places the important responsibility and duty of standing as trustees for the shareholders of the proposed bank and not allowing a single dollar of their money to be put in jeopardy in so far as the working of the bank is concerned until the provisions of the Bank Act are actually carried out-not carried out in a ' prima facie ' way, but carried out in a way which proves their actuality and reality. Now, I think all will agree with me that the incorporation could have lain here, if it had been allowed to, for 100 years, and nobody would have been damaged. The possibility of damage dated from the very day that the certificate was granted which allowed this force to be put in operation and the party to it, that was, and is, and will be held responsible for that certificate, is the party into whose hands it is confided by the Bank Act, namely, the Treasury Board. And if you come to look to the Treasury Board, as you look to a company or to a society, as to where the respnsibility lies, you will always find it lies in one or two, or at least in very few hands. In whose hands did this responsibility lie for the granting of this certificate which gave the power to Mr. Travers and his coadjutors to begin their operations? It lay theoretically in the hands of the Treasury Board; it lay actually in the hands of the Minister of Finance, and I call you, Mr. Speaker, to witness that

through this "whole discussion not a single allusion has been made by the. Minister of Finance to any other member of the Treasury Board. It was he who received the document, it was he who asked the opinion of the Minister of Justice, it was he who conducted the correspondence with Mr. McCarthy, it is he who signed the communications with Mr. Travers, he and nobody else, and it was upon his recommendation entirely that the certificate was finally recommended. Now, I think that commends itself to the minds of those who have heard this discussion as being in accordance with the facts. The things for us to consider, not only in the light of two parties sitting opposite each other, but in the light of the efficiency of tne banking institutions of this country, is to look very closely into the conduct of the Minister of Finance, which resulted in this certificate being granted. The Minister of Finance has based his defence on this: I had a ' prima facie' case, I took the evidence" given to me in that case, and if I did that I cannot be called upon to go any further; it is as far as ever was gone before in other cases. Well, I do not think that holds good. I do not think we ought to admit it, and for two reasons, one of which will be best ;put in the form of a question, I ask any member of this parliament if he had half a million dollars which he proposed to stake on a business venture, if he would stake that on the same quality of evidence and no more than the Minister of Finance had in connection with granting the certificate to this bank. I would not; the Minister of Finance himself would not. He said 'here to-day that he did not know Mr. Travers and never had met him before. Would he entrust half a million dollars to the management of Mr. Travers and gentlemen whom Mr. Travers might tell him were associated with him, when he did not know that a single one of these gentlemen was so associated with him, and when he did not know Mr. Travers himself and had never met him until a few days before the [DOT]certificate was granted? But, did not the Minister of Finance stand in exactly that position with reference to the $500,000 and more that was subscribed by the shareholders of this bank. Was not that money put in his hands in trust? The promoter of a bank comes to a man and the man says: yes, I will subscribe $5,000, because in this country up to the present time-I am not going to say it is so now- I feel sure that whatever happens after we all get together and are able to make our own board and manage our own affairs, whatever happens after that will be our fault, but up to that the Minister of Finance is my surety, first, that it will not be simply my subscription which goes in there
Mr, FOSTER
as bona fide, but that $500,000 with mine is to go in there as a bona nde subscription; it will not be only my money that will be paid up but it will be $250,000 which is bona fide put up, and until the conditions of the law are complied with my money is as safe as if it were in the bank, my money is in the hands of the Minister of Finance and it cannot be spent and cannot be squandered in any way. Now, that is the fair play which the Bank Act gives to any man; it is a guarantee that he is protected in that way. Therefore, I say the Minister of Finance should be equally as careful in connection with this money as he would be in the investment of the same amount of money for himself; he ought to be more careful for reasons which will commend themselves to the mind of any hon. gentleman in this House.
Now. the Minister of Finance had certain information, and it was his duty to come to a conclusion from evidence which was satisfactory to himself. I am glad to see that he does not depend on the opinion of the Minister of Justice, as some hon. gentlemen seemed to do when we discussed this question before, because he has acceded to the view that the Minister of Justice simply gave his opinion on the regularity of the papers, and that the matter of fact was to be decided by himself. So it must be. I ask the Finance Minister to correct me if I am wrong: If he asked the Minister of Justice for an opinion on the merits of the case, did he put before him all the information that had been brought to himself? He could have done nothing less if he was asking for an opinion on the merits. But he did not ask for an opinion on the merits. He simply wanted to know from the Justice Department if the papers were sufficient, and the Justice Department told him: The papers are sufficient, if you accept the evidence, for you to issue the certificate upon. The Justice Department threw back upon the Finance Minister himself the duty of seeing whether the evidence were sufficient or not. Now. note this, that the minister had his doubts in 1906 as to this bank. He has acknowledged that today. He said in 1906, after two failures to raise the funds:	My view was that they
were not the men to carry this bank to a successful conclusion, and I did not favour another extension. There is guard number one. The minister knew that this very outfit had attempted twice ^ and had failed to get the money, and two year's time had been spent, and he was of the opinion that if they could not get the capital in two years' time, they were not likely to be successful, and, therefore, he was against granting them another six months. So he was on his guard. Why should we, he said to himself bother with them any

longer? There is danger in it; don't let us grant them another term of six months. There was caution number one, and from that time on the Minister of Finance was bound, because of his own impression, to take especial care to see that_Jthere was bona fide capital, and nothing~~iess. But there was something else. The minister had knowledge in this case which I had not when I was Finance Minister. He wrote a letter to Mr. Travers on the 30th of November, from which I will read this extract:
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to us that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money.
The Minister of Finance had in his own mind, then, a knowledge that in previous cases there had been an attempt, whether successful or not-this letter would make it appear that it had been successful-to provide capital not in a bona fide way. but by the use of notes. There was guard and caution number two.. If there were nothing else, the Minister of Finance, as according to his own letter, should go below what was apparent on the surface. You notice his words:	' Where an application was in
all respects apparently regular,' this thing had taken place. Here was an application in all respects apparently regular, yet it might be wrong. Why did he not use the knowledge that he possessed to probe a little into this case to find out whether there was anything wrong underneath the ' apparently regular' application that was made? But the minister had more than that. On the 8th of October, on the 11th of October, and on the 19th of October, he had the letters from Mr. Leighton McCarthy. Now, the minister did not attach all the importance that I think is due to those letters. On the 8th of October came this letter:
My dear Mr. Fielding,-I have been consulted on behalf of a number of subscribers to the shares of the Farmers' Bank, and from the instructions I have received a number of the subscribers will dispute the bona fide character of the subscriptions.
Bear in mind the information that the minister already had. Here was another piece of information which said, not in previous cases, but in this case, some of the subscribers to this bank are going to dispute the regularity of the subscriptions. Mr. McCarthy's letter goes on:
I have not time to-night to give a full statement of the grounds of this request to you, but I beg to assure you that grave conditions have arisen which will require careful
consideration before the Treasury Board would grant any certificate for the organization of this bank.
There is no need of reading the rest of the letter; that is the pith of it. On the 11th of October, Mr. McCarthy had not received any word. He gets anxious, and he sends the following telegram to Mr. Fielding:
Please wire me assurance in reference to stay of certificate of Treasury Board mentioned in my letter of Monday night.
He gets the assurance from Mr. Fielding, and that is followed up by a letter from Mr. McCarthy confirming and carrying out the substance of his telegram. Then, on the 19th of. October there is this most important letter, which is more than a letter of information from a man. It is the actual transcript of an action undertaken before the High Court, which is more than gossip, more than rumour, more than what you meet with upon the street. I will read that letter:
Re the Farmers' Bank of Canada.
My dear Mr. Fielding,-I beg to inclose the special endorsement upon a writ of summons in the High Court of Justice for Ontario, which will be issued by: William A. Dixon, John Sproat, George Castle, William McLean, Finlay McCallum, Robert Hume, James Murray, George Denoon, John McLeod, Jane Shuert, William Harris, on behalf of themselves and all other persons alleged to be subscribers for shares of the capital stock of the Farmers' Bank of Canada who may desire to come in and be parties to this action, against the Farmers' Bank of Canada, James Gallagher, John Watson, John Ferguson, Alexander Fraser, Alexander Shepherd, Lown, W. R. Travers, C. H. Smith, A. G. H. Luxton, and the Traders' Bank of Canada, and W. J. Lindsay, and I respectfully request that the Treasury Board will stay any action upon the application of persons professing to act in the name of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, or in the name of the provisional directors of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, for a certificate under section 15 of the Bank Act on the grounds alleged in the inclosed special endorsement, and other grounds which may be disclosed upon the examination of the alleged subscribers for shares.
My hon. friend knew Mr. McCarthy, he had met him before, he knew him as a bright man of the party, and a good man in this House, and a stable man in the country. What does Mr. McCarthy say? He says:
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
[DOT]5335

That was special information, no rumour about that.
I wish you to have the kindness to acknowledge the receipt of this protest against the granting of a certificate so that I may advise the shareholders who are disputing their legality, and I would be pleased to go to Ottawa upon any appointment you may make for the further consideration of this matter.
What was the reply to that, and I want the minister's attention to this. This was dated October 23:
Bear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your_ letter of the 19th instant, to Mr. . Bidding's address, respecting the Farmers' Bank of Canada.
When application is made by the Farmers' Bank to the Treasury Board for a certificate to enable them to commence business, the representations contained in your letter with its inclosure will be laid before the board.
T. C. BOVILLE, Deputy Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance made a point as he thought, against my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) by saying:	You
are not quite right when you say that only three days intervened for examination, the application being made on the 27th November, and the certificate being given on the 3rd of the same month. The Minister of Finance said: Bear in mind that on October the 23rd the application was in, in the shape of a deposit of $250,000 to my credit. Now I will put this question to the hon. minister. From the 23rd October, 1906, until the 27th of November, 1906, will the minister say that either he or his department [DOT]took any step whatever to convince themselves of the bona fides of this application -or made any inquiry as to the standing or actions of the men behind it? That is a simple question, but there is a good deal in lit. I will go further. The information which Mr. McCarthy gave was to go before the Treasury Board. Let me *ask the minister if the Treasury Board met to consider this matter before the 30th of November, the very day when the certificate was granted. And I will ask him if he ever put before that board the information which Mr. McCarthy gave him, and which he declared would be put before them? That can be very simply answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot remember vdiat exactly happened between these dates.

My hon. friend has his deputy there. If the Treasury Board met, and if that board did consider that information, it must be on record, but I am just *asking him if that is not the case. So far as %ve can gather from the whole tenor of this thing, no investigation at all was made, either by Mr. Boville, the Deputy Minister of Finance, or the Minister of Finance him-

self or any other official with reference to the bona fides of this proposition. If I am wrong, that can be very easily shown. Mr. McCarthy's letter was accompanied by a document, and this is a copy of the document which accompanied it. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) tried to justify himself by saying that as Mr. Travers had assured him on the 27th of November that Mr. Beattie, of London, was a director, that was prima facie evidence of the respectability of the whole affair. But in this very document which Mr. Leighton McCarthy sent to the Finance Minister on the 19th of October, there occurs this as one of the indictments or one of the charges in this high court suit:
That Major Thomas Beattie, represented by the prospectus to have consented to act as a director, had not subscribed to any shares, and refused to be a director, and refused to allow his name to be used in any way in connection with the bank; and the plaintiff alleged that the names of other persons were represented by the prospectus to have consented to act as directors, who had not subscribed to any shares or given any authority for any such publication.
That was in the hands of the Finance Minister, and ought to have been in the hands of every member of the Treasury Board, because the minister had promised that it should he. Was it? What does this allege? On every hand it puts the minister on his guard. The minister seemed to think that there was nothing in this question, but this one point:	Were those who
were alleged to have been defrauded settled with? If they were, the objections were taken away and nothing remained.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

For the Finance Minister, everything remained, and what was removed was nothing, absolutely nothing. What remained?
