There remained the charge of fraud, the charge of misrepresentation, the charge of having directors on the prospectus who were not directors, the charge of paying immense sums in different ways that were unauthorized-all the grave charges that were made in the suit in the high court remained, and Mr. McCarthy could not and did not take them away. My hon. friend, the Finance Minister, knows that well enough. Did he read the judgment? The judgment was given on the 27th. What does it say, as clearly as any words can say it?
It says: On the 27th day of the month appeared before me, solicitors for both plaintiffs and defendants. The plaintiffs had been bought out and all their claims and obligations had been cancelled, and the two solicitors agreed to remove the case without costs. What does that prove? Would these men have been settled with if they had had no case? What was their

case? It was:	You got our names and
our subscriptions by fraud and misrepresentation; in one ease a man subscribed $1,000, and you put him down for $10,000. And other cases were specified of similar transactions. The defendant's lawyer comes and says to the opponent: Let's settle; we have bought out the plaintiffs. If you want to go to the evidence, you will find the evidence. Mr. Travers made a personal loan and sent Mr. Hunter and Mr. Lindsay out to the county of Hal-ton, bought out the claims, squared them up, took away the case from his opponent, and then came back into the court and a settlement took place. And any man who knows anything about these things could judge it to be nothing else than an absolute confirmation of the charges of fraud
Now, let me put one more case to the Finance Minister,-the confiding Finance Minister, the simple-minded. Finance Minister, the man who never looks below the. surface, but just sees what is on the top and if that is apparently all right goes no further down. He held in his hand the affidavit of Mr. Travers swearing to a list of bona fide subscribers as of that date who had subscribed what was put opposite their names and had paid what was put opposite their names. And, if he had taken the trouble to make the investigation, he would have found on that list the names of these very plaintiffs who had been bought out, who had no stock and whose names should not have been upon that list.
At six o'clock House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

And the plaintiffs allege that the acts and proceedings of the provisional directors were illegal and irregular; and the plaintiffs allege that the agents and solicitors professing to act under the name and authority of the provisional directors have procured a large number of subscriptions for shares, and have received the sum of $175,000 more or less on account thereof

What for?
-for the purpose of raising money to make a deposit with the Treasury Board of the Dominion government.
There were the resolutions spread on the minutes of the provisional directors' meetings, and all that the minister had to do when these warnings came to him was to ask for these minutes. He could have had them, and if he had had them this trouble would not have occurred. But it went further. On October 8, 1906:
Moved by James Gallagher, seconded by John Ferguson, that the provisional directors-
I want the House to note how far this, goes:
That the provisional directors execute a power of attorney to W. R. Travers for the purpose of endorsing all notes in their names as provisional directors and of signing their names to a note or notes for the purpose of raising funds to put up the deposit with the government, and we authorize the secretary to hand over all notes to W. R. Travers for said purpose.
Simple business precaution, especially when aided by the warnings to, and the premonitions of the Minister of Finance, by the statements of Mr. McCarthy, by the writ which was issued, by the result of that writ, would surely have advertised to the Minister of Finance that he ought to take, a little trouble to look into this matter to the extent at least of having the minutes of the directors' meetings in his possession. When Mr. Travers was asked in court why this last resolution was passed he was frank enough to say:	We could not
raise the money in any other way. That is October 8th; on October 15, Mr. Travers took $100,000 odd of'the notes of subscribers to the Trust and Guarantee Company, and made his loan personal of $81,000, and $80,000 of that went as a deposit as part of the $250,000 that was to be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance. But that was not enough. On October 22, he took other notes (not belonging to the subscribers to the bank), to the same company, raised a loan of $20,000, and had that by cheque sent to the credit of the Minister of Finance as a part of the $250,000 deposit. $100,000 of the $250,000 was not bona fide paid in cash by the subscribers; it was raised as a loan from notes they had given which might.
53-! 3

be paid or might not be paid, but which were jjiven absolutely in contradistinction to the doctrine of the Minister of Finance as well as to the express provisions of the Bank Act. Now, Sir, that evidence lay close at hand and was easily obtainable, and why in the world-can any one answer the question-with all these warnings, and with the means of getting the information, did the Minister of Finance not take the simple precaution to get it. Mr. Travers brought a stock list to the Minister of Finance, and he swore to it although the swearing was false. That was the stock list about which the Minister of Finance never asked the least question; he simply took Mr. Travers' statement that it was bona fide. Would it have been a difficult matter for him, to have asked Mr. Travers-about whom he knew nothing until three days before the certificate was granted-to kindly bring him the stock list as subscribed to by the subscribers, and if that list had been brought the -evidence was all over it that the stock list which was handed in by Mr. Travers was a fake list. How was it done? Mr. Travers describes it-They had not enough money in the early subscriptions, and the early payments to make the deposit; they went to work and gc>t notes from the subscribers, they discounted those notes and raised the money and they took the money thus raised, and to use their own language they spread it over the list of subscribers so. that the man who had not paid a cent was credited with one or two or three thousand dollars as paid. John Jones subscribed 10 shares, paid 10 per cent thereon and gave his note for the rest, the note brought in a discount, and the amount of that discount was not written down to this man, but it was placed to another man who had not paid anything. That, is the list that the Minister of Finance swallowed, that is the list he raised no question about, and all he would have had to have done was to ask for the original list, and he would find the evidence of the pencillings, and spreading on every page, but, he did not do it. There were officers and directors in that bank. How easy it would have been for the Minister of Finance if he had the least doubt, to write to some of these men and say: I find such and such a state of things, will you give me your view with reference to it. How quickly he would have got an answer from the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie). How quickly he would have got a.n answer from dozens and dozens of others. The Minister of Finance has very good financial friends in the city of Toronto; he could easily have written to any one of them, and they would have given him a proper estimate of what this matter amounted to, and what Mr. Travers amounted to. If he had written to any one of the mem-Mr. FOSTER.
bers of the Bankers' Association of Canada they would have given him that information, and would have been glad to have given it. The Bankers' Association is a part of the machinery of the Bank Act, and is at the disposal of the Minister of Finance for information, and if anybody can get information on these things the associated bankers can. Lying there for a month were three cheques, to the credit of the Minister of Finance, one from the Trust Company, for $80,000, one for $20,000, and one I think for the other $150,000; there they were lying in the Bank of Montreal to the credit of the Minister of Finance. Are those things so hidden that bankers do not know what is there? Do you mean t-o say that the question would not arise:	Why, if the Traders' Bank is
the bank of the Farmers' Bank do we have cheques from the Trust Company, and the information did get to the banking association as I shall soon show, and the Minister of Finance could have had the information just as easily as not. Did he ever ask any one for it? Now, he read Mr. Travers' affidavit. Let me just recapitulate. Mr. Travers makes an affidavit as to the acts of incorporation. They are plain; they are written in the statutes; he could not make a mistake about those. He makes an affidavit with reference to the prospectus. The prospectus was there to answer for itself- that is all right. But he says:
Now shown to me and marked exhibit 'D' to this my declaration is a list of the subscribers to the capital stock of the said bank correctly setting forth as to each subscription the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of shares subscribed for by him, the amount of such shares and the amount paid in thereon. Each of the said subscriptions is a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the said bank.
Travers swore to that; that was a lie. Mr. Leighton McCarthy told the Finance Minister a month beforehand that that was not so; and yet the Finance Minister says, what could I do? I had to take Mr. Travers' declaration. Mr. Travers also swears:
The provisional directors of the said bank on the said twenty-third day of October, 1906, caused $250,000 of the moneys so paid in and which actually had been received in respect of the shares of the capital stock of the said bank to be deposited in the Bank of Montreal to the credit of the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General.
Mr. Travers swore to that; it was an absolute falsehood. $100,000 of that was money that was not paid in by the shareholders, but was borrowed to make up the deposit under the condition that as soon as the Finance Minister let go the $245,000, this would be paid back, and it was.
At what interest?
10 per cent interest and a bonus of $1,000; and if I had been a lender of money, I should have wanted that much or more on that kind of security.
Who lent it?

The money was loaned by the Trust and Guarantee Company, and the bonus went to that company, accord-ins to the evidence. Mr. Travers then
swears:
I acted as secretary to the said meeting of subscribers holden on the said twenty-sixth day of November, 1906, and at the said meeting upwards of eighty subscribers were present in person.
According to the minutes of the bank 69 subscribers only were present in person.
The subscribers adopted by-laws for the bank, and elected nine directors duly qualified under the Bank Act to hold office.
They elected only eight directors, but a resolution provided that they should elect twelve. So that they did not elect the directors that were required by the law which they themselves declared necessary. Mr. Travers also swore:
The provisions of the Bank Act as to the subscribers to the capital stock of the said hank and the deposit with the Receiver General, and as to the notice of the said meeting of subscribers and the proceedings of the said meeting have been fully complied with and pursuant to the direction of the said meeting of subscribers and board of directors elected at such meeting, application hereby is made for the certificate of the Treasury Board to peimit the said hank to commence the business of banking in accordance with the said -let.
The minute book of that meeting and of the directors shows no resolution authorizing an application for the Treasury Board certificate, which would have been made clear if the simple precaution had been taken of having a certified copy of the resolution or of the minutes. I have already spoken with reference to the stock list. So that all the things that were essential, that were sworn to by Mr. Travers, turned out afterwards t-o have been falsely sworn to. The Finance Minister says, I could not know that at the time. But he could have taken the precaution to get corroborative evidence which was at his hand and easily obtainable., That he did not do. He preferred to take a simple declaration of a man whom he had not met until about three days before.
Now 1 come to that wonderful 30th day of November. I do not think any more eventful day than that has for many years dawned upon the city of Ottawa. Business was done with hurricane haste. If the departments of this government always worked with such speed and alacrity, there
would be no arrears in the government business of this country. On the 30th day of November an interesting number of people were in this city. Having made the deposit, having had the subscribers' meeting, Air. Travers makes haste after the 27th of November to come to Ottawa for his certificate. With him came Mr. Hunter and Mr. Smith, who had been the seejetary of the Provisional Board. Mr. Hunter came as the legal adviser of Mr. Travers. Mr. Smith came for a far different purpose. He had, figuratively speaking, blood in his eye or money on his heart, and he was to demand of Air. Travers, before that Treasury Board certificate was got, that he should be paid $2,500. or worse would happen. He employed as his lawyers Guthrie & Pringle of Ottawa. Guthrie & Pringle put the claim before Air. Hunter, who was acting for Air. Travers. In the end Guthrie & Pringle settled Smith's claim by taking an I. O. U. for, $1,800 from All. Travers who also had to pay the cost, $100; and, to use the expressive phrase of Air. Travers, ' I got rid of another difficulty.' When pressed to say why he should pay Mr. Smith, he supposed the reason was that Air. Smith knew the fraudulenc.y of the list, and that if he had told that to the Finance Minister, it would have been all up with Mr. Travers' application for the certificate of the Treasury Board. So that Air. Smith received his $1,800 of hush money, Alessrs. Guthrie & Pringle received their $100 of costs, Air. Smith hied himself home, and Air. Travers was happy once more. But a question arises here:	Did Mr. Hunter, or did
Messrs. Guthrie & Pringle know all the circumstances of the ease when they pried that $1,800 of hush money out of Travers' pocket and into the pocket of C. F. Smith? Air. Travers said they did. If so, that raises another interesting question. Now, all this was taking place on that 30th day of November. But here is a singular circumstance. On the 30th of November the Minister of Finance writes a letter to Air. Travers. Air. Travers says that letter was shown to Mr. Hunter. Air. Hunter left this city on the night of the 28th of November. How did Air. Hunter come to see the letter written by the Alinister of Finance on the 30th of November-how did he come to see it two days before the 30th November? If I understood the minister aright this afternoon, I understood him to say that he had previously told Air. Travers the nature of the letter he was going to send him. Then Mr. Travers must have had a conference with the Finance Alinister, and my hon. friend must have intimated to him what he was going to require from him in the shape of a letter, and must have told him that he would send him a letter on that line. Then, Air. Hunter, and

Messrs Pringle & Guthrie, who were both consulted1 about that letter, might have seen it two days before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The letter was written on the date mentioned, the 30th November, and nobody could have seen it two days before. Mr. Travers came to my department in connection with the certificate and I asked that he be sent in. In the meantime I had drafted a letter: to Mr. Travers, because I was not aware at the time that I could have a personal interview with him. When he came I discussed the matter with him along the lines I mentioned this afternoon, and I said to him that I was sending him a letter on the subject, and would like an answer. That was on the 30th of November.
Then my hon. friend had a conference with Travers previous to Travers receiving the letter, and yet the conference was on the 30th of November.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the same day.

I take the minister's word, but if I take that, the other ,mystery is unsolved, for I find this letter written from Toronto on November 29th, 1906:
W. E. Travers, Esq.,
Russell House
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Travers,-Mr. Hunter called in this morning, and I was glad to learn that so far things are going on nicely, and trust you will have no trouble.
Mr. Hunter went over all the applications and informs me that they are in first-class shape, and that he would have no hesitation in exhibiting them if called for. At his request I inclose three blank checks out of the check book in case you have occasion to use them.
Wishing you success, I am,
Yours faithfully, (Sgd.) .T. B. FITZGIBBON.
P.S.-Nesbitt has just called to inquire how things were going, and I have given him the gist of Mr. Hunter's report this morning.
So that on this 30th of November we have this interesting lot of business done. The Minister of Finance writes a letter to Travers in which, after regretting that he ,was not able to see him yesterday, which would be Thursday, the 29th-that was the date of the Budget speech I think-he says:
I was unable to meet you to consider your application for the issue of a certificate to authorize the bank to commence business.
Up then to November 30 the date of that letter, the Treasury Board had not had under its consideration the application for a certificate.
It was not the Treasury Board which was unable to meet Travers, but the Finance Minister. The Finance Minister takes the Mr. FOSTER
responsibility and no doubt is quite willing to take it. He goes on to say:
I shall be glad to see you to-day at my office at any time before one o'clock if you can call. Or I might be able to see you later, between four and five, at the House of Commons if that will be more convenient.
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to us that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which has reached us in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to us. I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers' Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
That is the letter to Travers. In a note written the same day, after he had explained the circumstances and got the opinion of Guthrie and Pringle upon that letter, Travers replied:
Ottawa, November 30, 1906. The Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Finance Minister, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-In reply to your letter of the 30th November, I have to say that in the case of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way mentioned by you.
Did the minister take that as an answer to his question? Surely not. What was the minister's question? It was this:
I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions to the Farmers' Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
He is told, not that this did not take place, but that the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way mentioned by him. And they did not, because in October and July they had given over the raising of money absolutely to Travers himself, and from that time forward Travers used their names, endorsed their notes to which he had signed their names, and got discounts 'in that way. Travers does not say that the money had not been raised in that objectionable way, but that the provisional directors did not do it. Did the Finance Minister take that as an absolute and definite answer to his question? If he did, I differ with him as to its being an answer at all. It is not an answer but an evasion which, though true in itself as

to tlie provisional directors, did not deny that the thing itself had been done as it really had been done by Travers himself.
Now, I asked my hon. friend to bring down the minutes of the Treasury Board meeting of the 30th of November. The minister brought down an extract, and the extract was that the Treasury Board had met and passed the application and had ordered the Treasury Board certificate to be granted. I then said to the Minister of Finance that it was not an extract I asked for, but the whole minute. And I got the whole minute. And the whole minute and the extract were exactly the same. Does the minister think that is an evasion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I desire to say, there is a printed form for extracts from the Treasury Board minutes, and the return was made on that form. The moment the full return was asked for, I inquired, and found that that was the whole record for the day.
I have the two, and I will give them to the Finance Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are both the same.
No, one is the full minute and the other is marked in writing ' Extract.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the usual form.

Printed; but this is written. Here you have it at page 27 of the Return, ' extract from, the minutes of a meeting of the Hon. the Treasury Board, held at Ottawa, on the thirtieth day of November, 1906." It is not an extract; it is the whole minute: nothing else was done that day. Now, what I asked the minister was, at what hour was that Treasury Board held, and he refused to give me the hour. Why should the minister refuse that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I told my hon. friend I did not know.
Mr. FOSTER No, the hon. gentleman refused to give it. I refer him to 'Hansard' on that point. If he did not know, he had his office behind him and could easily find out. Why did I want to know that? Tn the interest of truth. The letter to Mr. Travers says: You may see me up to one o'clock at my office, or you may see me at the House of Commons any time after four o'clock. When did Mr. Travers see the Finance Minister? Was it in his office before one o'clock, or was it not until after four o'clock in the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can answer that. It was in my office. I cannot give the hour, but, I should say, probably before the lunch hour. It was not in the House of Commons.
That is satisfactory. If the minister had told me that before-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr Foster) did not ask it.
I asked what hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He asked what hour the Treasury Board met, but not at what hour I met Mr. Travers.
Well, there is not much difference between the two, is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So long as my hon. friend understands it. 1 give him the facts.

If the minister had given me this information, it would have been just as good for me as the hour of the Treasury Board.'~Now, I wish to point out something else. The Treasury Board Act says that the Treasury Board shall consist of the Minister of Finance and any five other ministers. If the Act is lived up to-and if any Act is lived up to, this should be-there will be six members of the Treasury Board. But, by the return I hold in my hand, only three ministers are reported to have been present at this meeting of the Treasury Board on the 30th of November. If that be so, there was not a majority. The ministers noted as present besides the Finance Minister are Sir Richard Cartwright and Hon. Mr. Brodeur. Now, what I want to ask the Finance Minister is this:	Was the
Treasury Board regularly called for that day, or is this what we would call a hole-and-corner meeting, got up hurriedly? And when it was called and these three members were there, were the facts of the case in reference to this application, as the Finance Minister understood them, laid before the Treasury Board for its consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman wish me to answer? I cannot say exactly how that particular Treasury Board was constituted. With regard to only three members being present, I shall be happy to show the hon. gentleman: many occasions on which the Treasury Board business has been done with three members present. In that respect, there is ample precedent. What probably happened was that this Treasury Board took place at the Council. I wish to be very frank with the House about this matter. When there is abundance of time, the Treasury Board meets at my department, but we occasionally have a Treasury Board at the Council chamber where the members confer and agree upon what is to be done. But there are occasions, both with regard to matters of the cabinet and with regard to matters of the Treasury Board,

when it is not convenient or possible to get the members together, and you have to send information round and obtain the report in that way. My impression is that in this particular case the conference probably took place at the Council meeting that afternoon, but I would not speak definitely.
The minister does not say anything as to whether the precedent history of the matter was laid before the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The whole matter was probably discussed. As to what particular information was laid before my colleagues on that occasion I cannot say. Of course, they would ask for information and I would give it, I accept the full responsibility of advising my colleagues in this matter. They would ask my advice and I would give it.

That makes it all clear; we have now the modus operandi. I have only a few words more to say. The Minister of Finance says that the same evidence was accepted in this case as in other cases. I wish to ask whether there was any precedent case in which the circumstances surrounding an application were of the same nature as in this? The Finance Minister said; If I had denied this Treasury Board certificate, I should have been accused of not treating the farmers right. I do not think the Minister of Finance would take the position that, in order to parry criticism, or to keep himself from being wrongfully attacked, he should cease to perform his duty of guarding the interests of the shareholders which were confided to his trust. Which would the farmers like better-that he should make a thorough inquisition into this matter, and stop it on the demerits of the case and save them their money, or, for fear of criticism, should allow it to go through and them to be involved in this loss? _ There is only one answer to that question. It was the duty of the Finance Minister not to look at criticism one way or the other, but to perform his whole duty as the trustee for the shareholders, and that duty was to guard their rights. He says now:	I have been deceived. When
did the Finance Minister know that he had been deceived? He knew it, or had good reason to believe it, within twenty-four hours after he had granted that certificate, for there is the letter of Mr. Clouston, of the Bankers' Association, making the statement in black and white that he had reason to believe that this denosit was not a bona fide deposit and that therefore steps should be taken to prevent the bank going into operation. Tf, within twentv-four hours of issuing this certificate in 1906 the Minister of Finance knew that he had been deceived, what has he done up to the present time to punish the men who deceived M. FIELDING.
him? Is it to go forth that in this administration men, in a matter of this kind, can combine and deceive the Minister of Finance, and by reason of that deception bring ruin upon hundreds and thousands of people, and yet the Finance Minister and the government not stir a hand to ferret out and punish the men who deceived him?
Why, Sir, Mr. Clouston wrote a letter on the very day that the Treasury Board issued the certificate. That came to the minister the next morning, the minister read it in his mail. Under that allegation by Mr. Clouston there was only one thing for the minister to do. He had given a cheque for $245,000 of the shareholders' money to Mr. Travers, and it was his duty simply to advise the bank not to honour that cheque, and to have written or telegraphed to Mr. 'Travers that he wanted to see him immediately, to have brought him here, and to have had that matter thoroughly explained before he allowed the shareholders' money to go into the hands of Mr. Travers. More than that, he knew that the associated bankers sent their man, Mr. Knight, up to Toronto, and Mr. Knight investigated in Toronto, and came to the conclusion that the deposit had been made with borrowed money. He telephoned Mr. Burn, Mr, Burn communicated with the department; and yet, with both Ml. Clouston and Mr. Knight, and the evidence standing out before him, he took no steps to collar that money and to prevent the bank from going into operation. If I am rightly informed, the bank did not open its doors to do business until the 2nd day of January, 1907. On the 18th of December, Mr. Knight made his report to Mr. Burn, and Mr. Burn presumably made his report to the Finance Department, and even then the Finance Minister did not do anything. The bank was not in operation, the money would have been saved, this gigantic series of mal-deeds vcould all have been impossible.
The minister says that the bank failed on account of bad management. Even though, he say's, $100,000 of capital had been depleted, yet afterwards, he does not know quite when, the capital did begin to come in. Good management would have saved it, bad management was its curse. I go back a little further than that, and I say that a bad manager rvas the curse of that bank, a bad manager was the very man that could have been unmasked by my hon. friend and put out of business, because every transaction that he took in the formation of that bank was accompanied by perjury, and fraud, and misrepresentation. If the Finance Minister had taken hold of it and unmasked Mr. Travers and his operations, there might have been bad management, but it would not have been bad management by Mr. Travers, because Mr. Travers would have been impossible as manager of any

bank. There is where I think my hon. friend made a great mistake. Look at it. He had his own opposition to the extension: warning, premonition, No. 1; the other cases previously occurring in his mind, to his knowledge: warning No. 2; Mr. McCarthy's letters, and the judgment: warning No. 3. The appeals and conversations of my hon. friend from Halton, whose word I am bound to take, for this consideration, that while the Finance Minister is busy with many things, my hon. friend from Halton though a busy man, lias less business, and would be more likely to follow this matter out in the interests of his constituents. So without any disrespect to the Minister of Finance, I would say that I am bound to think that my hon. friend beside me would not have made the mistake he has made in regard to his memory of those things. But Sir, will the Finance Minister tell me and tell this House that had no other warnings? I asked him again the question whether any of the officers of his department had had interviews and warnings. He never answered that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer at once. I certainly had no other warnings-I do not know what my hon. friend refers to-I had no warnings that have not been brought to the notice of the House in the discussions that has taken place.

Very well, then. I will make what I think is a practical test of that question. My hon. friend has said that there is no work for a commission in this matter, the courts will do all the work that is necessary to be done. I deny that all the facts can be brought out in a police court examination. It does not seem to me that the most important part of the investigation into this business can be or will be taken up in the courts. There is a lot of information which lies at the very essence of this matter that the courts will not look into at all. And with reference to all that has taken place in granting the certificate, my hon. friend dismisses it with the simple statement that it is all a matter of record. It is not all a matter of record. I want to put the gravity of this case before my hon. friend and my right hon. friend. Up to this occurrence, the people of Canada had absolute faith that when the Minister of Finance granted a certificate for a bank to go into operation, everything was perfectly square. They had perfect faith. Have thev now? It is absolutely shattered, and until something is done, and a thorough investigation is held, coupled with legislation wherever legislation is needed, to strengthen the preliminary operations, until the truth of the matter is brought out, this country will not have faith in any bank which is put into a position to do work through the Department of Finance of Canada. I believe it is absolutely necessary, no matter
whom it hits or whom it hurts, to have a thorough investigation into everything connected with this matter. I would go further, and take in all the banks that have failed during the last four or five years, the curators' reports of which furnish strange reading to any jjerson who will go through them.
I ask the government to grant that royal commission which my hon. friend has asked for in his motion, and I will bind myself to add material evidence in the line of the evidence of my hon. friend from Halton, if an opportunity is given me before that commission. There is other evidence to be brought out, give us a tribunal and we will bring it out. Who is to be hurt by granting this commission? Who can be injured? The government does not mind the expense of it. It is easy to get able men to carry it out; it can be carried out without great trouble and much time. What reason is there at all why it should not be granted? We ask that it be granted. There are questions after questions that we would like to ask the officers of the department, the Finance Minister and the members of the Treasury Board, and numerous others. If there was a tribunal before which these could be put, all the facts could be obtained. Why should we not have that information? It is not for the benefit of my hon. friend or of myself. It is not to pull one down and build another up, it is to get the absolute facts of the case? Why should we not have the commission?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has said that his constituents are troubled over this matter of the Farmers' bank, many of them having become shareholders, many of them having deposits and many of them having suffered severe loss. The hon. gentleman says that it is expected that he shall do everything here that he is able to do. lit is the right of every member of this House to keep himself squared with his constituents in any way that he legitimately -can and perhaps this is not the only instance where men have occupied an hour or two of the time of the House in an endeavour to square themselves with their constituents at home. The hon. gentleman has said that the name of this bank-the Farmers' bank- won the confidence of the people of his constituency and of the country. It may be that there is something in that, but I take it that there was a great deal more in the prospectus that they issued to the public and in the representations made by smooth tongued and skilful canvassers who were engaged in the selling of the stock. I notice by the prospectus that one of the features of it is the statement of the large -eturns that have been made by Canadian banks in times past. I find a list of twelve

and then go on, organize and do business Sec. 15 of the Bank Act says:
No certificate shall be given by the Treasury Board until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the Board, by affidavit or otherwise, that all the requirements of this Act and of the special Act of incorporation of the bank, as to the payment required to be made to the minister

The payment of $250,000 had in this case actually been made.
-the election of directors

The directors had been elected in the regular way,
-deposit for security for note issue

The required deposit-of $5,000 had been made to the minister.
-or other preliminaries have been complied with

The other preliminaries, so far as appeared by the affidavit, had all been complied with.
-and that the sum so paid is there held by the minister.
The $250,000 and the $5,000 had been so paid and were so held by the minister. So that as far as all the evidence made it appear, every single possible requirement of the Bank Act had been complied with. But, I am told that the affidavit which the Act stipulates may be accepted, and it is the only specific proof the Act mentions, was not sufficient and that further evidence ought to have been asked for. I claim that the position of the Minister of Finance in this respect is not different from that of the Provincial Secretary in the Ontario government or the Secretary of State in the Dominion government when a number of business men apply for a charter in the one case under the Dominion Companies' Act or in the other case to Mr. Whitney's government under the Ontario Company's Act. They show the particulars on printed forms furnished them for that purpose. They show the names of at least five shareholders, the names - of the provisional directors, the amount of stock subscribed, the amount of cash paid in on the stock, and these statements are verified by affidavit of one of the promoters or interested parties. The member for North Toronto says that the minute books of the company might have been obtained and they would have furnished evidence that the certificate ought not to have issued. 1 would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) or any other man who has occupied the position of Minister of Finance in the Canadian government, whether in any single instance the minute book of a company has been asked for under similar circumstances?
Was there ever a case like this?
Yes.
When and where?
There was no case different from this.
Name a single case like this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My recollection is
that there was no case of the minute book being required previous to this, although in a recent case I think we did require the minute book. I am safe in saying that in no case prior to this was the minute book required or demanded.
Was there ever a case like this before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that substantially this case is not different from other cases before the board, except in one case where I know a certificate was granted without an affidavit at all,

There were 250,000 good reasons in the shape of the $250,000 deposited to show the bona fides of the men en- _ gaged in the transaction. That was far " better evidence than any affidavit as to the bona tides of these people. A quarter million dollars is not easily picked up, and there was no source whence the greater part of it could come than from the shareholders of the bank and from the shareholders of the bank it did come. Mr. Travers did not and could not put up $250,000 of his own money; it was obtained from the shareholders of the bank' who had subscribed to the stock of the bank. The Minister of Finance has pointed out, and none can deny it, that at this time Mr. Travers had as good a reputation as a financier and man of integrity as has any member of this House. He had been manager of the important branch of the Merchants' Bank in Hamilton, and I am informed that when he left the employ of that bank he took with him from the general manager a splendid testimonial in the shape of a letter speaking highly of his integrity and financial ability. Long after the certificate had been issued and the bank opened for business, the government of Sir James Whitney showed their confidence in Mr. Travers and in the Farmers' Bank by depositing in that bank Ontario government funds to the amount of $25,000. Talk about a trusteeship; the Ontario government were trustees for this $25,000 of public money, and they deposited it in the Farmers' Bank, showing the confidence they had in the institution and in the men by whom it was managed. Mr. Travers, who at that time had the reputation of being an honest business man, was manager of the bank, and the



president at that time was Dr. Beattie Nesbitt, in whom, at least a large number of the people [DOT] of Ontario had confidence. The Ontario government and Sir James Whitney had such confidence in him that they made him registrar in the city of Toronto. Therefore, not only had the general manager of the bank a good reputation at that time, but so had the president of the bank, and, in addition to that, some of the directors and shareholders were amongst the foremost business men of Ontario. The hon. member for Hastings asked was there ever such another case as this, and he proved there never was by his sarcastic laugh, and we were told by the hon. member for North Toronto that the letters from Mr. Leighton McCarthy should have aroused the suspicion of the Minister of Finance. Let us look at the letters. The first says that Mr. McCarthy is representing eleven subscribers of stock in the bank and on the 9th of October he writes:
My dear Mr. Fielding,-I beg to inclose the special endorsement upon a writ of summons in the High Court of Justice for Ontario, which will be issued.
* This would seem to contradict the statement of the hon. member for North Toronto that the writ had issued because Mr. McCarthy says that the writ would be issued, and the inference is that when Mr. McCarthy obtained satisfaction for his clients the writ was withheld. But, Mr. [DOT] McCarthy does not ask the Treasury Board not to issue the certificate; what he asks for is delay. Mr. McCarthy was acting for eleven shareholders whom he named, and ' for all other persons alleged to be subscribers for shares of the capital stock of the Farmers' Bank of Canada _ who may desire to come in and be parties to this action.' Apparently no other subscribers did come in and the eleven subscribers represented by Mr. McCarthy so far as we know were the only ones dissatisfied. The hon. member for North Toronto speaks of these eleven men having been bought up, which implies that they were bribed not to proceed with the action they intended to proceed with. Well, these men had subscribed for the stock of the Farmers' Bank, and I would not wonder that my hon. friend from Halton or some other equally cautious and shrewd man had advised them that their investment instead of being sure to be as protfiable as they expected, was attended with certain risks.
They then thought it wise that they should withdraw, and if possible escape any liability. They engaged Mr. McCarthy. He proceeds to threaten, and possibly he may have issued a writ. The promoters of the bank say: We do not want any delay or litigation; we will go to these eleven dissatisfied shareholders, and we will give Mr. MILLER.
them back the money they have paid in, and take over their stock. These eleven subscribers had subscribed for stock to the value of $23,500, but they had only paid on that stock $6,530. So that all that the promoters of tie bank had to do to stop the agitation of these eleven men was to raise $6,530, which they did, and took over their stock. Now, Mr. McCarthy's letter shows that eleven men out of a total of 557 subscribers were dissatisfied. There were at the same time 546 other subscribers who apparently were perfectly satisfied with the investment they had made, and were not making any trouble or asking for any relief. These 546 satisfied subscribers had subscribed stock to the amount of $476,500. Now, what were the irregularities pointed out in Mr. McCarthy's letter? The sole irregularities on the part of any person up to that time were that certain subscribers to the stock of the bank who had supposedly paid in $6,530 had not paid in all of that in money, but had paid a part of it in their promissory notes. Had these farmers and others, instead of giving their promissory notes to Mr. Travers, taken them to some bank and discounted them, and paid the money to Mr. Travers on their stock, they would not have been guilty, morally, legally or otherwise, there would have been_ no irregularities to point out, and no technical reason why they could have evaded their stock subscription. The hon. member for North Toronto asks:	Would the Finance
Minister in the transaction of private business, have invested $500,000 of private funds in the same careless way? I say, in reply to that, that the Minister of Finance did not invest one single dollar of that $500,000, and he was not in any way responsible for the investment of that or any part of it, to any subscriber of that stock. The man who was responsible primarily and above all was W. R. Travers, and what position did he occupy, and how did he obtain that position? He was general manager of the bank. He had not been made general manager by the Treasury Board or by the Finance Minister, but by the votes of the 557 shareholders including the shareholders in the county of Halton. They are the men who had given to W. R. Travers the responsibility and the right of handling their money. The hon. member for North Toronto says that the Finance Minister was a trustee, or the Treasury Board were trustees, for the handling of the money, and the hon. member for Halton uses to some extent the same reasoning. He said that if the Treasury Board had refused to issue the certificate, then the $250,000 deposited with the Treasury Board would have been refunded, and could have been paid back to the shareholders. That is not the case. The $250,000 had been paid in by W. R. Travers. If the Finance Minister was a trustee at all,

or if the members of the Treasury Board were trustees at all, then surely they were trustees to those who had made the application for the $250,000 paid in, under the law, to the Treasury Board. But I direct the attention of the members of the House to section 17 of the Bank Act, which says:
In case no certificate is issued by the Treasury Board within the time limit for the issue thereof, the amount so deposited shall he returned to the persons depositing the same.
Who in this case was W. R. Travers? Then, subsection 3 of section 17 says:
In no case shall the minister be under any obligation to see\ to the proper application in any way of the amount so returned.
So not only does the Bank Act not say that the Treasury Board or the Finance Minister are trustees for the $250,000, but it takes especial care, in the plainest and most definite language, to say that they are not trustees for that $250,000, and cannot be so regarded. Then surely they cannot be held to be trustees for a single dollar of the money of the bank. The hon. member for North Toronto says that the. hon. Minister of Finance could have had information and advice from the Canadian Bankers' Association, which would have put him upon his guard. I say that if the Bankers' Association, before the certificate was issued, had information which the Minister of Finance ought to have had, and which would have influenced him in the granting of the certificate, then they had not only a financial and a personal interest in seeing that the Finance Minister obtained that information in time to be of some use, but also a public duty in seeing that the information was given to him as quickly as possible. But the Bankers' Association, if they had that information, which I doubt, withheld it until after the certificate had been issued. I ask again if the hon. member for North Toronto, during the time he was Finance Minister, ever asked for the production of a minute book of a bank applying for a certificate or of any other financial institution applying for a charter or a license authorizing it to do business. We believe, and the people of this country believe, that the Minister of Finance is a very careful and capable official; but we do not claim that he is a seer or is omniscient. It is all right now, after loss has come, and there has been calamity, to endeavour to blame the Minister of Finance, it is all right to say that Mr. Travers made an affidavit that was utterly false in this particular, and that particular; but there was no possible way by which the Minister of Finance or any other mortal man could at that time have known that the statements contained in Mr. Travers' affidavits were not correct.
169i
Suppose that this parliament had known years before the certificate' was issued, as they know to-day, that Travers was not an honest man, what would have been the power of this parliament and the power of the Treasury Board? I say that the Banking and Commerce Committee, when the charter for this bank was being obtained, might very well have considered the character of the men who were promoting the scheme. I say that the members of this House, who were called on to adopt or reject the report of the Banking and Commerce Committee, might very well have considered the character and business ability and prospects of the men who were asking for incorporation. The Banking and Commerce Committee is composed of members on both sides, many of whom have large business experience, and all of whom have no doubt the interests of the people at heart. Of that committee my hon. friend from Halton is one of the most careful and efficient members. I say that that committee might have refused a charter of incorporation to Travers and his associates if it had any reason to doubt his character or ability. And after that committee had agreed to give these men a charter, the members of this House could still have refused to pass the Act. But when this parliament, under the advice of the Banking and Commerce Committee, did issue a charter to these people, it was beyond the power of the Treasury Board to withhold the certificate because of the character of the men applying for it.
Travers had nothing to do with getting the charter.

It does nor make any difference whether Travers had anything to do with getting the charter or not. The members of the committee or of this House can refuse a charter to any one applying for it, but the Treasury Board, once a charter is given, cannot refuse a certificate after the parties have complied with the conditions of their Act of incorporation. In this case, the conditions were complied with to the letter in every particular.
We say that they were not.

I say further, suppose the Treasury Board, with its six members, had taken upon itself to say that they had information as to the character of these men or their lack of business ability and would not issue to them the certificate to enable them to do business, what would have happened? Would this House have been disposed to _ accept that position of affairs? Would this House be willing to delegate to any set of six men, no matter who, the right to pass judgment on the character or ability of any group of men to whom this House had given an Act of incorporation? In this

case Travers was a member of the Conservative party, Dr. Nesbitt, the president of the bank, was also a prominent -member of that party; and if the Treasury Board had gone out of its way to refuse a [DOT]certificate to these men, the Minister of ^Finance and the other members of that board would have been accused of having been actuated by political reasons in withholding that certificate.
I do not think that anything can be accomplished by a Royal Commissioin. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has had the privilege ot examining all the correspondence and all the documents in this whole matter, and I do not think that any commission could make a more searching inquiry into the facts than he has done. Hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is well able to make an investigation and examine every bit of evidence submitted to him, which is all that could be submitted by this House to a Royal Commission.
There is a lesson to be learned in this, and that is that we, as a parliament, should be more careful when we come to frame a new Bank Act, and I refer, hon. members . opposite to the new Act drafted by the Minister of Finance. If they will compare the sections of that new draft Act with the parallel sections of the present law regarding the issue of certificates, they will find that the hon. minister has taken many precautions to guard the interests of the public more fully than they are in the present law. But I repeat that every member of this House, who was a member of it when the old Act was passed, is equally responsible with the Minister of Finance for the Act as we have it to-day.

Perhaps it is just as well that I should read the amendment before the House, as it is some time since any reference has been made to the real question at issue. The amendment is as follows:
This House is of opinion that a Royal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate the incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, and the granting of a certificate by the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to issue notes and commence business, and all circumstances connected therewith and generally to inquire into and investigate the operation and efficiency of the Bank Act in relation to the affairs and transactions of the said hank.
I am free to admit that when an amendment such as this is brought before the House, the responsibility rests on those who bring it forward of making out a prima facie case to justify an investigation. But it would be idle to expect members on this side to prove the point they wish to have investigated. Of course, however, in order to compel even the hon. member who Mr. MILLER.
has just taken his seat (Mr. Miller) when he comes to read the amendment, to vote for it, as I hope he will, it is necessary that we should show that there is something worth investigation in the transactions referred to. What are the circumstances which we say justify an investigation? The people of this country, through their representatives, have provided that after parliament has granted a charter to a bank, that bank has no power to carry on its business until it has complied with certain formalities. But after it has complied with these formalities, the Treasury Board is allowed to give it a certificate, and on that certificate-and that alone-can it begin business. A great deal has been said about the shareholders, and I do not intend to add to what has been said on their behalf. But what about the depositors? The Minister of Finance may possibly say that he was led astray by Travers, the representative of the shareholders? But what has he to say about the unfortunate depositors throughout the land? What has he to say of those men who were in comfortable circumstances a few months ago and who are to-day in the depths of poverty because the hon. minister blundered. In my own constituency, I met an old soldier, about 75 years of age and his wife of the same age. This man had worked hard during 20 years since leaving the army and accumulated a little property, but he had deposited his savings, some $11,200, in the Farmers' Bank in March last, and all he had left after all. these years of industry, was $3. It is such people as those, people who put their money into this bank relying on the Minister of Finance seeing that the law was complied with to the letter, who say, surely we are entitled to an investigation. I am not implying that the Finance Minister himself was corrupt in any respect; but I do say that if he has any proper regard for his own reputation, he should be the first man to ask for a complete investigation into all the circumstances which, to say the least are most extraordinary.
Now, there are certain facts which cannot be gainsaid. They have been laid before the House very fully by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), but perhaps I may be allowed, briefly to Tefer to some of them. In the first place, as I said before, the responsibility is, by statute, thrown on the Treasury Board. The statute provides that $500,000 must be subscribed and $250,000 paid up, bona fide payments in cash, and certain other conditions complied with without the performance of which the Treasury Board has not the power to grant a certificate. Now, I would like to ask the Finance Minister, sitting in this House to-night:	If he had
known on the 13th day of November, 1906, all that he knows on this 15th day of March, 1911, about the state of affairs at the former

date, would he have granted that certificate to the Farmers' Bank of Canada? The hon. gentleman declines to answer

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not decline to answer. I thought it did not require an answer. Certainly, with the information now available, I would not have issued the certificate.
Well, we have got that far. The hon. gentleman admits on this 15th day of March, 1911, that he issued a certificate under such circumstances that, had he known

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can all be wise after the event.

But the Finance Minister was the one man who had it in his power to have the information that would make him wise before the event. And I desire to call attention to the care, persistence and assiduity with which the hon. gentleman prevented his own eyes being opened despite every effort to that end on the part of those who were in possession of the facts. That 'is the reason why we are entitled to an investigation, to find out what hypnotic power was around the Finance Minister on that unhappy 30th of November, 1906. It was well known that those connected with the bank had had a great deal of difficulty in getting the required stock subscribed. The time of the charter had been extended. I think, twice. So, if ever there was an occasion on which the Finance Minister, on the merits of the case,_ might well have been justified in looking into the facts, it was this case. But, while proceedings were on, a letter was received by the department from one of the leading lawyers of the city of Toronto; I presume the Finance Minister read this letter-or he did not. Might I ask: Did the hon. gentleman take the trouble to read that letter and the information

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The information was conveyed to me by my officials in substance.	,

Then, we find, in substance, the Finance Minister knew that the writ was about to be issued. The names of all the parties were given, some 10 or 11 of them; the grounds of the action were fully set out in the endorsement of the writ, which I will read in a moment, and also stated in the letter itself. In the letter it is stated that this action was to be brought. It says: I
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received
and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
This is information coming from a reliable source. He goes on;
I wish you to have the kindness to acknowledge the receipt of this protest against the granting of a certificate so that 1 may advise the shareholders who are disputing their liability, and I would be pleased to go to Ottawa upon any appointment you may make for the further consideration of this matter.
That was written on October the 19th. The department hurried to reply to it four days later-they acknowledged the receipt of the letter. On the 19th of October, then, this writ had not been issued. On the 31st of October a letter was written by Mr. Bo-ville, the Deputy Minister of Finance, to Mr. McCarthy, in which he said:
Referring to your letter of the il9th inst.-
The one I have just mentioned.
-addressed to Mr. Fielding, on the subject of the Farmers' Bank of Canada and the issue of a certificate to that bank to commence business under section 15 of the Bank Act, I notice recently a reference in the newspapers for a judgment given by Judge Anglin in a suit relating to this matter. In view of the decision rendered, I shall be obliged if you will let me know if you still desire the protest contained in your letter to be brought before the Treasury Board upon an application of the Farmers' Bank for a certificate to be considered.
Was a more remarkable letter ever written? A leading lawyer states facts which the minister and his deputy should have been delighted to receive, if they were facts, and which, if true, disentitled the Farmers' Bank to receive this certificate. This letter made it the duty, beyond all question, of the deputy minister to investigate. Because no one will suggest that when the Banking Act provides for a Treasury Board consisting of the Finance Minister and five of his colleagues, it intends that five wooden Indians with a rubber stamp can transact the business of the Treasury Board. There must have been a presumption somewhere that a little intelligence would be used. And when parliament requires certain conditions as prerequisite to a certificate being issued, surely it expected that the ordinary-I do not suggest extraordinary-amount of intelligence and industry would be displayed by the officials in carrying out that law. Yet, after this extraordinary statement, the only letter of inquiry is to ascertain if, the suit having been settled, this 'lawyer is prepared to withdraw the protest , he had entered for these 10 or 11 gentlemen. But not u. thought of the hundreds of shareholders and thousands of possible depositors, but'only of the few individuals whose names happened to be mentioned in that writ. It may not be out of place to give a few of the principal

charges made, to show how serious this matter was. This is the endorsement on the writ:
This action is brought by the plaintiffs on their own behalf and on behalf of all other alleged shareholders of the Farmers' Bank of Canada who dispute the validity of alleged contracts to take share of the capital stock of the Bank, and who allege that they were induced to subscribe for shares through fraud and misrepresentation, and who may request to be joined as plaintiffs. And the plaintiffs' claim is: (1) for a declaration that the alleged contracts are void: (2) for the rescission of alleged contracts to take shares of the capital stock of the Farmers' Bank of Canada; (3) for an accounting for the money or promissory notes received-or alleged to have been received-in the name and on behalf of the provisional directors of the bank; (4) for an injunction; (5) for a receiver; and (6) for administration. And the following are the particulars of the plaintiffs' claim.
il. That the Farmers' Bank of Canada was incorporated by special Act of the parliament of Canada, passed on the 18th day of July, 1901.
2. The defendants, James Gallagher, John Watson, John Ferguson, Alexander Fraser and Alexander Shepherd Town, were appointed by the said Act to be the provisional directors of the bank.
Then it recites how the bank was proceeded with, prospectuses issued and stock-books opened. And these are the charges of impropriety:
11. The plaintiffs and others subscribed to shares, and the plaintiffs allege: (1) that the provisional directors who professed to act for and in the name of the bank had no lawful power or authority to receive subscriptions for shares or to accept them; and (2) that the subscriptions for shares which were procured from the plaintiffs and others were procured through fraud and misrepresentation, and the plaintiffs allege, amongst others, the following particulars of fraud, namely:
1. That the agent in procuring the subscriptions for shares falsely represented that persons had subscribed for a larger number of shares than they had in fact subscribed for, and the following are examples of such false representation, namely: (a) that Robert Noble whose name is entered in the prospectus as one of those who had consented to be a director, had subscribed for shares to the amount of $10,000, whereas he had in fact only subscribed for shares to the amount of $3,000; (b) that John Sproat had subscribed for shares to the amount of $10,000, whereas he had in fact only intended to subscribe for shares to the amount of $1,000, and that he was induced to sign an application in the belief that it was filled up for $1,000 and that the general manager afterwards claimed that it was a subscription for'$10,000, and the said Jchn Sproat then repudiated the entire subscription; (d) that James Murray had subscribed for shares to the amount of $10,000, whereas he had in fact only subscribed for shares to the amount of $1,000.
(e) That Dr. Stewart was subscribing for shares to the amount of $10,000, whereas he was not in fact subscribing for any shares;

and other false representations of a similar character were made by the solicitors and agents in reference to alleged subscriptions of other persons.
Then there is a charge with regard to Major Beattie, which was read before. Then there are a number of attractive inducements held out, and then it is alleged that actions and proceedings were taken, and so forth. Now surely there wercj charges enough to put any treasury board on its guard, charges explicitly made, and charges which went to court; and when we find that on the 19th of October the writ had not yet been issued, and that on the 31st, the Deputy Minister of Finance could write that the judgment had. been given which, as a matter of fact was given on 'the 27th of October, and when we find all these allegations of fraud against the provisional directors and general manager, that when the writ was not issued on the 19th of October, such haste was made that the judgment was entered on the 27th of October, and the judgment itself recites as follows:
And it appearing that the said plaintiffs John Sproat, George Castle, William A. Dixon, William McLean, Finlay McCallum, Robert Hume, James Murray, George Denoon and John McLeod, have assigned and transferred their applications for the issue of shares of stock of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, and their right to shares in accordance with the said applications, to one William J. Lindsay, and that the claims of the said plaintiffs last above named, and also the obligations and liabilities of the said plaintiffs, have ceased

2. It is ordered and adjudged that this action be and the same is hereby dismissed out of court without costs.
Now, Sir, if a deputation had come from Toronto with a brass band to serenade the Finance Minister, and had come with the express purpose of calling his attention to the fact that these charges of fraud had been made by Mr. McCarthy and had been substantiated, they could not have given a better evidence of the fact than this judgment which was referred to by the Deputy Minister of Finance in his letter of the 21st of October; and after these people had been settled with, and after these charges of fraud had been made, the minister simply inquired whether the individual whose clients had made these charges and who had been settled with, wanted to press this protest; but that the minister owed any duty to the shareholders or to the people of Canada, never even seemed to have entered his mind. Well, we find then that Mr. McCarthy received back his papers, and there was an interval of time, and then Mr. Travers sends in his application for a certificate and makes his declaration on the 27th of November. Now when the minister had seen the endorsement in this writ, and when there were 8

or 10 plaintiffs in that case whose names were before him, and when Mr. Travers on the 27th of November, this judgment having been entered on the 27th of October, makes his sworn declaration, that on which the minister gave, and could only give, the certificate, would it be believed that neither the minister, nor the Treasury Board, nor anybody in the department took enough interest in the proceedings to read the declaration of Mr. Travers to find out whether these men were still on the list given by him as shareholders on the 27th of November. If he had, he would have found their names still there, and then surely if he had so learned, he would have taken some steps to prosecute the man who had perjured himself in making that declaration. If the minister had only taken the trouble to read the papers put before him by Mr. McCarthy, the papers on which alone he. granted the certificate, he would have found that the applicant was a perjurer, and he would surely have been justified in refusing to give to a perjurer a certificate to do business, and all this calamity, and all this loss and suffering which has been entailed on many people of this country, would have been saved; but all this exists to-day because the minister declined to take the trouble to read these papers, or if he did read them, declined to convey the information to the Treasury Board. On the 27th this declaration was made, and it would seem that Mr. Travers came post haste to Ottawa, and apparently a little deputation with him, and if we are to believe what was said by the hon. member for North Toronto, he was here on the 30th of November. Now it is a peculiar thing that the depositors' money had been paid into the Bank of Montreal about a month before. On the 23rd of October the money was paid into the Bank of Montreal, then suddenly on the 30th of November, when the minister was up to his eyes with his budget speech, Mr. Travers and his friends came down here, though it has been said that they had been here for two or three days already; at all events, on the 30th of November, when there was still plenty of time-the certificate did not require to issue until the 18th of January-on the 30th of November there was such urgency that this certificate should be issued, that that very day the minister, in his bustle, and hurry, and excitement, writes to Mr. Travers, and let us see what the minister wrote on the 30th of November to Mr. Travers:
Dear Sir,-I regret that owing to pressing engagements yesterday, arising out of the budget, I was unable to meet you to consider your application for the issue of a certificate to authorize the Farmers' Bank df Canada to commence business. I shall be glad to see you to-day, at my office, at any time before one o'clock, if you can call. Or I might be
able to see you later, between 4 and 5, at the House of Commons, if that will be more convenient.
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring to your notice so that you may consider it at once.
' A phase of the matter,' only that and nothing more.
It has been represented to us that in soma previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some case the subscribers did not actually pay in cash, but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which has reached us in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to us. I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers' Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up, have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
Now is it conceivable that, unless there is something which we do not know, which is not before. the House, and which we would like to investigate, is it conceivable that after receiving such an extraordinary endorsement of a writ from Mr. McCarthy, that when Mr. Travers was applying for his certificate, when he had put in his declaration, the minister fails to read the declaration for fear he might find the list of shareholders which would show the declaration was false, he writes to Mr. Travers and he is so afraid of this financial magnate, that he actually fails to refer to any charges made against his bank, and in the most timid way intimates-what? He intimates that: My attention has been called to the fact that we have been fooled by these declarations before; this is not the first time we have been fooled, we are alive now, we are alert to-day, and we are determined that we will not be caught againt by a false declaration, we will check your declaration by asking you whether it is true or not. I wonder if an investigation would not be justifiable, even to find out the process of logic by which the minister thought he was going to get the truth of a statutory declaration by asking the man who made it whether it was true or not. I think the amendment might be altered so as to give the committee power to inquire into the simplicity of the Finance Minister, to inquire into the reasons of the Finance Minister for making this bargain with Mr. Travers. It is no wonder that we wonder at his capacity for making bargains. But that is not all. This letter was written to Mr. Travers asking him for an answer, and as the member for North Toronto pointed out, the Finance Minister did not even get what he asks for. He was

apparently assiduous in his care to ask a question that would be easy for Mr. Travers to answer, and Mr. Travers did not even answer that question. Now the minister ventures to intimate that in the case of the Farmers' Bank of Canada the provisional directors did not raise the money in the way mentioned by you. That is the kind of close, rigorous cross-examination and checking of the affidavit that the Finance Minister enters upon; he decides that the certificate must be given and so it was given. We have really nothing to do with the Finance Minister in this case except that he is chairman of the Treasury Board and except in so far as the correspondence shows that he acted. Our charge is not against the Finance Minister; we want to investigate what took place before the Treasury Board. What has been said by the Finance Minister?-It's not fair to say that the Treasury Board knew anything about the charge which was made.
He took the responsibility.

It is all very well for the Finance Minister to say that he took the responsibility. He might do that had the statute put it in his power, but the statute says that the Treasury Board shall do so and so. When the statute says the Treasury Board that does not mean the Finance Minister, and when it says the Finance Minister that does not mean the Treasury Board. So, we have first the Finance Minister deliberately shutting his eyes to all the information given him, then we have him writing Travers not saying a word to him about this case, but referring to some suppositious case in days gone by, we have been calling attention to the fact that he had been deceived by declarations heretofore, he asks a question which is not answered, and then runs off to the Treasury Board. He does not even know where he met them, he could not tell whether he met them in his office, or in the council chamber, or where it was, but in some way he met these worthy gentlemen and the Treasury Board agreed to issue this certificate. One would have thought that the Minister of Finance would have been anxious about that certificate. Not he The very next day he found a letter from bir Edward Clouston, president of the Bank of Montreal and head of the Bankers' Association, and Sir Edward Clouston puts his case very clearly. Surely a man in the position occupied by Sir Edward Clouston is entitled to a little consideration and respect when he makes a serious charge.

T. C. Boville, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Farmers' Bank of Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-In connection with the application of the Farmers' Bank of Canada for the usual certificate from the Treasury Board, I have reason to believe that the money lodged, or to be lodged, at Ottawa as stock subscriptions, cannot be regarded as paid-up capital, and that a large proportion of the amount necessary to the obtaining of a certificate is a loan made upon the promise of its payment when returned by your department.
That surely is a specific enough charge.
Permit me to request that, if only for the protection of the public

Like myself, he has a feeling for the unfortunate depositors.
-the Treasury Board will exercise its right to refuse to issue a certificate if it thinks best so to do, until a thorough investigation has been made into the circumstances stated herein.
When the Finance Minister received that letter, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) pointed out, what in the world was there to prevent him from stopping the payment of the $245,000 cheque and demanding back that certificate which had been obtained by fraud? If the general manager had refused to give it back, clearly there are courts of law in the land. He could not possibly be allowed to keep it under such circumstances, and, having obtained this certificate by fraud and perjury, it is not to be imagined that the courts were powerless to cancel the certificate. The Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board had ample knowledge from Sir Edward Clouston that the whole institution was a fraud, that they were not entitled to the certificate, and that therefore the certificate which the Treasury Board wilfully and knowingly gave was a certificate that was not justified by the law of the land. Now, the case would seem to be so reasonably clear so far that an investigation is a small matter. The fatuity with which the Minister of Finance seemed to have followed all the directions of this man Travers is most remarkable. It was not very long after that that the minister received a letter from a very honest young man. At page 29 of the Return we find the following letter addressed to the Deputy Finance Minister;
The Farmers' Bank of Canada, Milton, April 7, 1907.
