Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Will you kindly give me your opinion as to the following: Our general man-

ager sends to the different branches lists of notes given in payment of onr capital stock. These notes he makes the managers put through as discounts, crediting the amount to
H.	O. This is figured in the government return as paid-up capital and circulation issued to that amount. If I read the Bank Act correctly, section 76, he is asking us to do what is not right. That is written on April 17th anil gives such a shock to the department that it is two weed's before they recover. On May

Dear Sir,-I have received your letter of 1st instant and inclose as requested one of the notes which I referred to in my letter to you of 17th ult.; when we renewed these-notes we dated them 2nd Jany., '07, or later, and made them payable at this office.

I looked all through the book carefully trying to find any further comments, but that note seems to have been a crusher. Apparently there is no further correspondence between Mr. Vankoughnet and Mr. Boville or the Minister of Finance. But we have the fact then that on the 3rd May that letter was written and received on the 4th May giving the minister this information. The letter of Mr. Vankoughnet told about notes being discounted at his office by the manager and the proceeds credited to the head office and he wanted to know whether this was in accordance with the law of the land. He stated that the
amount under discount in his office was $111,885, In that one little office in Milton the Finance Minister knew that on the 4th May, 1907, there were $111,885 in discounts of note which had been given for the capital stock. Now, in the meantime not only had Mr. McCarthy questioned it, but Mr. Knight had been very busy. Some demands have been made and so the department is screwed up to the point of venturing to ask for another Return from their friend Travers, and they got it. We have it here on page 35 of this Return. There the minister is told that:
The portion of the $375,473 paid-up capital of the bank, as per Return of March 30, 1907, represented by promissory notes of the shareholders, held by the bank, amounts to $59,110.
That is the sworn declaration of the general manager. On the 10th May there was received by the Minister of Finance the sworn declaration of W. R. Travers that the total amount of these notes held by the bank was $59,000, while the minister had under his thumb the letter from Mr. Vankoughnet, the manager at Milton, saying : ' I have in my branch notes under discount to $111,885, my conscience smites me and I appeal to you as Minister of Finance to let me know if I am doing what is wrong.' How can this House account for the fact that away back in May, 1907, the Minister of Finance had it proved up to the hilt by documents in his own possession that Travers had perjured himself again? Where was the difficulty in bringing this bank to its senses? What possible use could there be in getting bank returns month after month from a man who already had committed, deliberate, wilful, ridiculous perjury? The Minister of Finance does not come before the House and say: I laid that before the Treasury Board, I was over-ridden, they would not listen to me, but he comes here and says: I take all the responsibility. Does he appreciate the responsibility to the widows and orphans of this country who have suffered because of the actions of two classes of men-those who have robbed the people and are now represented in the penitentiary, and those who have failed in their duty to enforce the law of the land-and who have refused to take a single step to save the shareholders and the depositors?	_
Surely if ever there was a case which would justify investigation it is this, and if ever there was a man who would hail with joy the opportunity of investigation it is the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance must not forget that if in the face of this extraordinary evidence showing the knowledge brought home to him again and again and again and refusal on his part to act, he calls his supporters in and votes^ down an amendment asking for investigation into the circumstances which

led to the issue of this charter, he may not be surprised if strong comments are made in the country and perhaps very great injustice done to himself. There may be a perfectly honest explanation of all this, and I do not say there is not, but I do isay that if the Minister of Finance refuses to give men an opportunity to believe the simple, innocent, plain, convincing facts, he cannot be surprised! if people draw their own conclusions which perhaps would not be gratifying or complimentary to him. Now, Sir, the last speaker (Mr. Miller) said that the Treasury Board had to give the certificate, and that the very best guarantee that all was well was the presence of the $250,000 deposit. Imagine a man, in the face of what has taken place saying that that is any guarantee. What are you to think of 'that for logic? Why should this House be compelled to waste time listening to a man who in the face of what has taken place in regard to the Farmers' Bank would deliberately tell this House in the year 1911 that the best guarantee that could he had was the presence of this $250,000. I think, Sir, that the Treasury Board would be bound to grant a certificate to the bank if after making all due inquiries they were satisfied the provisions of the Act had been complied with, but they made no inquiry in this case and they simply wrote a letter to the Justice Department in which they invited just the answer they got. Why they should have gone to the Justice Department at all I do not know; perhaps it is because they always do. An the question submitted to the J ustice Department was a peculiar one. Again and again attention had been called to the fact that there was something rotten in the state of Denmark and instead of looking into the actual facts, on the 28th of November a letter was written to the Deputy Minister of Justice which reads :
E. L. Newcombe, K.C.,	-

Ottawa, Nov. 28, 1906.

certificate to commence business under sections 13-17 of the Bank Act, and papers in support thereof.
You ask me to advise you if on the papers submitted such certificate may legally issue.

Did you ever hear of a Crown attorney or a judge before whom a charge was made against a man of stealing or of having committed a fraud sending for the man and saying:	I have

The Minister of Finance, the Treasury Board, do not seem to have realized their position at all-do not seem to have realized the responsibility resting on them to protect the public, as suggested by the president of the Bankers' Association, There is some reason for the issue of this certificate which has not yet been made known. If the Minister of Finance had acted as a man of ordinary intelligence under the circumstances-I am speaking guardedly, Mr. Speaker-I submit that where a man oome3 before the Minister of Finance asking for power to open the bank, asking to be placed in a position where he can fleece the public of millions of dollars, where the Minister of Finance has been told that this man has already committed many frauds, I say a man of ordinary common sense and intelligence, acting in the interests of the people, would have insisted upon evidence other than that of the man who is making the application himself. I must give the Finance Minister credit for the fact, as he states it, that he did not receive the letter from the president of the Bankers' Association until the day after this certificate was issued. I have no doubt that the Treasury Board, authorized to issue a certificate, had the inherent power to cancel that certificate, if they were satisfied afterwards that it was unwarrantedly issued. We have no evidence that the Minister of Finance took the slightest notice of the warnings that he received from the president of the Bankers' Association the day after.
Did he take the advice of the Department of Justice then?

I am not aware whether he did or not. It is not on record, and we have nothing here to-day except

that which is on record, and there is a great deal that is not on record. Now, I have no hesitation in making the charge, I believe the people of this country will make the charge, that the losses that the depositors and shareholders of the Farmers' Bank have sustained are morally owing to the culpable negligence, the criminal negligence, of the Treasury Board. They made a mistake, to say the least of it; certainly they failed to exercise that common sense and that intelligence that any man would who had in his heart the best interests of the people of this country. And having got further evidence, he would have refused to authorize these people to open their doors and be in a position to bleed the public to the extent of millions of dollars. I believe, therefore, it is the duty of parliament to do something for these people. I do not know, I am not prepared to say, that - they would have a legal claim against the Crown, because the Crown is supposed to do no wrong, by a monstrous fiction. But these people, having suffered this immense loss by reason of the negligence of the Treasury Board of this government, this government is morally responsible for the losses they have sustained, having taken the course they did.
The Finance Minister says that Mr. Travers came to them as a man that they did not know anything against. Well, that was simply a negative quality, we do not generally trust a man in large transactions of whom we know nothing. This man was charged with a dozen frauds of a very serious character, which may possibly involve millions of dollars. We do not know the man at all, and we accept the word of this man in the face of these charges, and send him out authorized to rob the people of this country as he has done. Now, Sir, I submit that the people of this country, especially those who are interested in the Farmers' Bank, especially the depositors and shareholders, desire to know all the facts in connection with this matter. They are perfectly satisfied that we have not got all the facts this afternoon. The conduct of the government cannot be explained on the facts we have, but their conduct may be explained on other facts. Who introduced this man to the Finance Minister? We have it stated that the chief whip of the Liberal party at that time did so; I think that is not denied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not recollect whether it was or not. But whv should not anybody introduce him? There was an article to that effect in a Toronto paper, it may be quite correct. I do not know.

We would like to know, the public would like to know, they have a right to know, all the facts in connection with this matter, what it was that influenced the Treasury Board to issue a certificate under these very suspicious circumstances without making any inquiry whatever to corroborate the statement made by the gentleman who is making the application. As I said a few moments ago, the issue of the certificate I believe to have been illegal. There was no quorum of the Treasury Board qualified to issue a certi-cate. Of the capital stock of $500,000, $250,000 not having been paid in cash by the subscribers, they were not legally qualified to do business. There is a case which I think establishes that fact, the case of Cass against the Ottawa Agricultural Insurance Company and others, reported in volume 22, Grant's Chancery Reports, where it is held that where a company was required by statute, to raise $50,000 before beginning business to be paid in by those who have subscribed to the stock, and where they borrowed a large portion of that money to make up the $50,000, they were not legally authorized to do business. That is the case here. Those who subscribed for this stock did not put up the $250,000. One can understand why the statute requires subscribers to pay the cash. A later section of the Act provides for double liability in case of insolvency; it therefore becomes important that the shareholders should be men of substance, and hence it is required that they should put up the cash, not simply to give their promissory notes. The most superficial investigation on the part of the Finance Minister would have disclosed that the subscribers had not put up the $250,000, and therefore they were not entitled to the certificate. If the Finance Minister had taken the reasonable course, and had found they had been guilty of fraud in the inception of this institution he probably would have said to them: I shall have nothing more to do with you. It has been shown that you are capable of an attempt to defraud the public, and so far as I am concerned you will never be authorized to open a bank anywhere in the Dominion of Canada.
I take much pleasure in supporting this resolution. I believe the people require ,a thorough investigation, and I submit that this House should not surrender its right to investigate a matter of this kind because it is in the police court of Toronto or in the hands of a curator there. It is the duty of this parliament to investigate a matter where the officials of this parliament, the Treasury Board which is composed of six members of the cabinet, have shown themselves guilty of negligence in not taking a reasonable course to satisfy themselves that there was no fraud in the matter. If they had taken that course no certificate would have been issued, and thousands of people who have suffered seriously would have been spared. I, therefore, submit that a Royal Commission should issue that we may get all the facts, no matter who is. hit or who is hurt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not intend to occupy much time, because the subject which is engaging the attention of the House has been very thoroughly debated. This is one of the most disastrous bank failures that has ever occurred in Canada. Looking at the statement of the curator one sees that the liabilities of the bank amount to nearly $2,000,000, and looking at his statement of the assets there will be' apparently a shortage of $1,250,000 to $1,500,000. The capital stock is gone, and it is doubtful whether the ordinary creditors will receive anything at all, and in any case they are not likely to receive more than a small percentage of their claims. The failure has occasioned widespread distress not only throughout the province of Ontario, but elsewhere in this country, and in the United States. I have received a good many letters on the subject; oge of them is so cogent in its terms and so well written, that I will take the liberty of reading it to this House, because it expresses in respect of one locality what has occurred in many localities in the province of Ontario, and elsewhere in this country. This is a lady writing from Lakeside post office in Ontario. She writes in this way:
I write to you on behalf of the ' Farmers' Bank.' I wrote some time ago to Mr. Lau-rier, also to Mr. Fielding on this subject, and both sent short but courteous replies. I read all the parliamentary discussions this year, and when the time comes for the Banking Act to be ventilated in parliament, come to the rescue and plead the cause of the poor widows and people either paying for, or renting farms, who have lost their whole savings in this bank. Some are in want who are advanced in years, while others cannot meet their payments this spring. If you were to visit Embro and heard the tales of distress, your heart, I am sure, would be touched with sympathy. Our butcher lost $2,000 in it at Lakeside, which he took out of the Imperial in Ingersoll for convenience. His sons have both been through operations this last year, and here this man is without a dollar, and his oldest son and son-in-law are on rented places lately set up and cannot meet their payments, and this, sir, is repeated wherever Travers set his trap.
Then she goes on to speak of criminal proceedings at Toronto, commenting upon them and wanting to know why they are not more effective. She proceeds as follows: I
I am proud of my country, but I am ashamed of the way this affair is conducted. Now, sir, if yon know any other of the members who know better than you how people are suffering, do please get them to advocate the rights of the people and pay them their hard earned money. Those who stole should be made to refund, and what the Keeley mine does not supply, should be raised by the government, and paid by May at the farthest. You know very well that the people have no Mr. CROTHEES.
way of agitating reforms of any kind but through their public men, both in church and state, and I feel that this has been a clear case of robbery, and is a case of truth and justice, to be rectified by the government, and also things should be put on such a basis that such rascalities could never occur again. You know the government helped the sufferers by the Martinique disaster, and it is quite right, but how much more should our own people, who are industrious and law abiding, be helped, who put their money in the * Farmers' Bank ' believing it to be chartered properly. How soon we should be arrested and fined heavily if we made wine and sold it without paying license to the government. A pedlar cannot travel a one-horse wagon without paying license, and why should bankers be allowed so much liberty which has often driven sufferers to the lunatic asylum hr worse than all to suicide. I do hope you will do your best in this matter, and oblige thousands.
That gives an idea of the way this matter is regarded throughout the country, of the suffering which has been brought upon the people, and the question is: How has all this result been brought about? The bank obviously should not have been permitted to commence business. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance himself has admitted that. There can be no doubt at all, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, that if he had taken the ordinary business precaution of calling for the minute books of this bank, as one would suppose that any man in his senses would have done, he would have seen that the Bank Act was being violated, he would not have permitted the bank to commence business. Let us see what the real conditions were when the bank commenced business. I am not speaking of my own knowledge; I am taking it from the curator's report, at pages 6 and 7. of the Eeturn which has been brought down. The directors had collected about $211,000 from subscribers in cash. In contravention of the law of this country, a fact that was shown by their own minute books, which were not brought here as they should have been, they paid out improperly for commissions and expenses $41,000; so that they had in actual cash not $250,000, but $170,000. They handed over that $170,000 and turned over subscribers' notes to W. R. Travers, who borrowed on these notes $80,000, which amount, with the $170,000, made-up the $250,000 which he deposited with the Receiver General. Travers then handed back the $80,000 which he had borrowed, and thus the bank's capital, after the deduction of the $80,000, did not amount to the sum required by law. Further than that, the actual amount of capital, $211,000 which had been collected by the directors, was further diminished to the extent of $41,000 which it had been improperly paid out. How was it possible under such conditions that the Treasury Board permitted

this bank to commence business? Had the Treasury Board any notice that these unlawful acts were being perpetrated? They had the most direct and positive notice, I affirm, in the presence of the Minister of Finance, and I will prove that the notice of the frauds was never from first to last withdrawn.
Mention has been made of the oral notice given to the Minister of Finance by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), I can only say with regard to that, without the slightest disrespect to the Minister ol Finance, without any desire to impugn his sincerity, that where you have two men, one of whom deposes to a positive and direct recollection of a particular incident, and the other of whom says he has no recollection of that incident and does not believe that it ever took place, according to' well recognized rules which prevail in courts of justice, assuming that both of these men are sincere in their statements, credit must be given to the man who has a positive and direct recollection and credit will not be given to the man who simply says that he has no recollection.

Well, I accept the minister's statement at once. I only mention it because it came to me in a way that seemed to give some appearance of credibility. But, we need not debate these things. There was the letter of Mr. Leighton McCarthy, there was the writ, and the endorsement upon the writ itself which, in the plainest and most unmistakable terms, conveyed a warning to the Minister of Finance in this regard. Perhaps sufficient emphasis has not been laid upon one particular paragraph of Mr. McCarthy's letter of the 19tn of October, 1906, three days before the writ was issued. He stated the writ would shortly be issued, and three days afterwards on the 22nd of October, it was issued, and in his letter he says:
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons professing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes arid received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
The intimation conveyed by that to any one who is familiar with the provisions of the Bank Act is simply that these men were conspiring together to contravene and to evade the provisions of the Act which the Minister of Finance was bound to see observed. From first to last Mr. Leighton McCarthy, in the correspondence at least, has never withdrawn the statement made by him in that letter of the 19th of October,



1900. True, he did in a subsequent letter state that his clients had been settled with, but he never in any letter withdrew these statements of fact which he made to the Minister of Finance. The statements in the writ itself are so startling and convey so plain a notice to the Minister of Finance that one would think there could not be the slightest doubt in his mind as to what his plain duty would be. The first charge of fraud is this:
1. That the provisional directors who professed to act for and in the name of the hank had no lawful power or authority to receive subscriptions for shares or to accept them; and (2) that the subscriptions for shares which were procured from the plaintiffs and others were procured through fraud and misrepresentation, and the plaintiffs allege, amongst others, the following particulars of fraud, namely:
1. That the agent in procuring the subscriptions for shares falsely represented that persons had subscribed for a larger number of shares than they had in fact subscribed for, and the following are examples of such false representations.
Then he gives eight or ten cases where men had applied for small sums and had been put down for sums ten times as great, and where men who had subscribed nothing at all are put down on the stock list as actual subscribers. In all the instances so set forth in this writ, as I understand it, the names of these men are on the stock list which the Minister of Finance accepted on the sworn declaration of Travers, although comparison of the writ with the list would have given the plainest possible indication to the Minister of Finance not only of fraud in the first instance, but fraud persisted in up to and at the very-time when this certificate was being asked for from the government:
That Major Thomas Beattie, represented by the prospectus to have consented to act as a director, had not subscribed for any shares, and refused to be a director, and refused to allow his name to be used in any way in connection with the bank; and the plaintiffs allege that the names of other persons were represented by the prospectus to have consented to act as directors who had not subscribed for any shares or given any authority for any such publication.
Was it not open to the Minister of Finance to write a letter to Major Beattie and ask him whether that statement was true or false? Was it not competent also for the Minister of Finance to have taken the precaution which Major Beattie took to have looked up the record of Mr. Travers a little and to ascertain whether this matter was not worthy of further investigation by him. There is a further direct charge of fraud which ought to have attracted the attention of the Minister of Finance in an especial manner:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And the plaintiffs further allege that the agents and solicitors who were procuring subscriptions for shares had not lawful power or authority to solicit or accept applications for shares or subscriptions for shares.
And the plaintiffs allege that the agents and solicitors professing to act under the name and authority of the provisional directors have procured a large number of subscriptions for shares, and have received the sum of one hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars more or less on account thereof, and have also procured promissory notes to be signed by persons who were subscribing for shares, payable to the provisional directors of the bank, and the persons acting in the name and under the professed authority of the act of incorporation and amendments thereto, are endeavouring to discount or procure a loan by the transfer of the said notes.
And the plaintiffs further allege that the persons professing to act as aforesaid under the alleged authority of the provisional directors have unlawfully deducted large sums of money for alleged services and commissions and other purposes out of the money received by them.
The plaintiffs allege that the shares and the money and the promissory notes procured from them have been procured through fraud, deceit and misrepresentation.
Finally in the concluding part of the endorsement prayer is made for:
An injunction to restrain the bank, and the provisional directors and the general manager, and their officers, servants or agents, from the publication of a notice to call a meeting of the alleged subscribers of the shares of the capital stock of the bank, and from making application to the Treasury Board for a certificate under sections It and 15 of the Bank Act.
The defendants in that suit under the terms of the settlement in court admitted in effect every one of the charges of fraud I have just now read.
I am not going into particulars of Sir Edward Clouston's warning just at this moment, but to be brief let me sum the whole situation in this way. The minister had the following warnings-in the first place he had the warning of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). Again I repeat that, attributing equal sincerity to each, the testimony of one who has a distinct recollection of a particular incident which impressed itself upon his memory, is always to be accepted against that of the other party who merely affirms that according to his recollection the incident did not occur. In the second place he had the warnings of other similar witnesses who can be produced if inquiry is granted. In the third place he had the warnings of Mr. Leighton McCarthy in the three letters referred to. In the fourth place he had the warnings contained in the writ of summons, and the endorsement. I want to point out to the minister and to the House that the charges

in that writ were of a two-fold nature, namely, those which concerned the plaintiff alone and those which concerned the public interest, and the duties of the Finance Minister. Among the latter were the charges that moneys had been illegally paid out by the provisional directors in contravention of the Bank Act, thus impairing the hank's capital. Even if the plaintiffs were settled with, was not that a consideration which should have been before the mind of the Minister of Finance, and which should have impelled him to call for the minute books, and for every scrap of evidence which would bear upon the conduct of the persons which had been promoting the organization of this bank. Another charge made by Mr. McCarthy, and which never has been withdrawn was: That notes of subscribers had been and were being discounted by the provisional directors in order to evade the Bank Act, and to deceive the government, and there was a further charge that fraudulent representations were being made by this man to obtain the money necessary to secure the certificate of the Treasury Board. And, although Mr. McCarthy withdrew his clients' objection to the granting of the certificate by the Treasury Board he never withdrew his statements and representations which disclosed a fraudulent attempt to evade and contravene the Bank Act. Although the suit was settled the allegations of fraud set forth in the writ were never withdrawn, but were rather confirmed by the judgment of Mr. Justice Anglin. The written warning of the Canadian Bankers' Association confirmed all previous warnings, and the Treasury Board should have instantly ordered the return of the certificate and failing compliance the government should have peremptorily ordered the issue of a Royal Commission to. investigate the alleged frauds. The Treasury Board had a plain and clear duty before it. We have been asked what could the Minister of Finance do? In the first place he could have ordered the production of the minute books, he should have ordered an investigation, he should have ordered further corroborative evidence, he should not have granted that certificate after warnings which had been conveyed to him unless he was absolutely and positively assured by the evidence as to which there could be no doubt whatever that everything in connection with the Farmers' Bank had been properly done in accordance with the law, and that no fraud was intended upon the government of this country or upon the public. That is what he should have done. But, he says he was helpless when the direct and positive warning of Sir Edward Clouston came to him. I say he was far from helpless.
What should he have done? He should have sent a telegram after Travers. It is 1701
said that he sent a messenger after him, and that Travers refused to give up the certificate. That may be mere rumour; there may be nothing in it; and I do not vouch for it. But the minister should have sent a telegram after Travers ordering him to return that certificate immediately and telling him that if he failed to comply, the government would the next day issue a Royal Commission to inquire into all the circumstances attending the organization of that bank and its application to the Treasury Board for a certificate. That is what the minister could have done, but that is what he did not do; and as the direct result of his inaction and neglect, the farmers of Canada, the workingmen of this country, have suffered losses to which they should not have been subjected; the Bank Act of Canada, as to its efficiency and its operation, has received a blow such as it never received before. From one end of this country to the other people are in doubt to-day as to our banking system, seeing that under the operation of that system, under the safeguards which ought to be observed by the Finance Minister and his department, these frauds have been perpetrated. The minister had Travers' affidavit, it is true, but he had the warnings of reputable men that that affidavit did not set forth the true statement of facts. What was the course he took? He took the solemn and serious course of asking Travers in private conversation whether or not his affidavit was true or false, and he received of course the answer that the affidavit was true. He then solemnly determined that that conversation should be made a matter of record and sat down and wrote a letter to Travers and Travers wrote a letter to him, and then he handed over the certificate. Is it any wonder that the other side of the House has lapsed into silence over this transaction? I do not wonder that they no longer have the courage or hardihood to stand up and say a word in defence of the position of the government. I do not wonder that the Prime Minister left this chamber in disgust and only returned a few moments ago. I wonder whether we shall hear from him; but if we do I sincerely trust that he will give some attention to some of the serious matters which have been urged against the administration of an important department of his government in this connection.
Then, as my hon. friend from Hastings has observed, within two or three months after this bank had begun business, the Minister of Finance learned out of the mouths of officers of the bank, by direct statements under their own hand, that these notes which had been discounted for the purpose of raising part of the capital paid over to the Receiver General, were still being held at different

branches of the bank. At one branch $109,000 of this paper was even then being held and that was only two months after this bank had begun business. That was confirmation, if any was necessary, of the warnings the minister had been given. It was confirmation of the warnings given by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), by Mr. Leighton McCarthy, by Mr. Osier and other persons, by the writ of summons and the endorsements thereon, and last but not least it was confirmation of the direct and positive warning given by the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association. What was the object and. purpose of that association when its president conveyed to the minister the positive statement that a fraud was being practised on the government in order that a greater fraud might be practised on the people, if not to induce the government to take some course to protect the public. Yet the minister remained inactive and matters were allowed to drift. This is absolutely an indefensible case, and it will be to the discredit of the government if it should refuse the inquiry demanded by my hon. friend from Halton.

In approaching the discussion of this question, I think it is advisable in the first instance to examine what are the objects stated by the motion of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). The motion reads:
That this House is of the opinion that a Rcyal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate tha incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada and the granting of the certificate by the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to issue notes and commence business, and all circumstances connected therewith, and generally to inquire into and investigate the operation and efiiciency of the Bank Act in relation to the affairs and transactions of the said bank.
In this motion three things are asked. It asks that a commission should be appointed to investigate the incorporation of this bank, its organization and then the granting of the certificate by the Treasury Board permitting it to issue notes and begin business. The discussion which has already taken place has already eliminated from this motion two of the objects sought to be accomplished by it. The first thing to be examined was the incorporation of the bank; but if I understood the speech of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that part of the motion has been abandoned because he said that in reality there was nothing to investigate as regards the incorporation of the bank.

If my right hon. friend will allow me, I was combatting the argument made by the Minister of Finance. He Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
divided the motion into three sections, namely, the incorporation of the bank, the granting of the certificate and the operation of the bank. I agreed with him, that as far as the incorporation by the commission and this House was concerned, ail were responsible. My hon. friend from Halton said that by incorporation he meant all the preliminaries up to and including the granting of the certificate. I was simply replying to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that this is really a distinction without a difference. Will my hon. friend tell me now, in the face of the discussion we have had, what would be the object of an investigation into the incorporation of the bank? What would such an investigation lead to? The same thing applies to the organization of the bank. The Teal crux of the matter is the third part of the motion, the granting of the certificate by the Treasury Board. All the discussion ^has1 really been upon this part of the motion and nothing else. Nothing serious has been said about the incorporation or organization, but the whole complaint has been that the Treasury Board -advised by the Minister of Finance, made a mistake in granting the certificate. Therefore we can eliminate the other two parts and address ourselves to this alone, namely, what are the facts connected with the delivery of the .certificate? My hon. friend from Halton made his motion with an object, and that object was to show that the certificate had been issued erroneously, that it should not have been issued at all, that the Department of Finance and the Treasury Board had been deceived and all this led to the conclusion that the government or parliament or the country should assume the losses incurred- by the shareholders-. I think I have stated _ the case fairly when I pat it in this way. We are asked to- investigate the granting of the certificate in order that such investigation might lead parliament to come to- the rescue of those who lost their money in this institution. If siuch be -the case, let U3 examine the reasons given why parliament should take this extraordinary step. The reason given is that the Department of Finance was deceived. All the speeches made, even the speech o-f my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Borden, Halifax), have been to this effect, that the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance, as leader of the Treasury Board, issued a certificate which should not -have been issued1, that the government had been deceived, and -that those who 'lost by the bank should not bear their losses but they should be borne by the country.
Deceived in what manner? That is the question we have to investigate. That the

Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board have been deceived was admitted long ago. But let us go further. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) tells us that this is only a preliminary step leading to another whereby parliament should be induced to come to the rescue of the men who put their money in the hands of Mr. Travers and the other directors of the bank. In what manner have the department and the Treasury Board been deceived, and what had the deception to do with the ultimate loss incurred by the shareholders? The deceit consisted in Mr. Travers, manager of the bank, reporting under oath that the bank had received in cash $250,000, half the amount required to be subscribed under the statutes. There iis no longer any question about the deceit. When Mr. Travers declared that the shareholders had put into the treasury of the bank $250,000, that was deceit to the extent of about $80,000. That is admitted. Afterwards the bank failed. The question arises: Was that deception the cause of the failure of the bank? Can any one say-I put the question to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax)-that this deception was the cause of the failure of the hank and the loss of the shareholders' money? I believe it has been stated and not denied that ultimately the whole of this money was paid into the treasury of the bank. There was a deception at the time, but afterwards the whole $250,000 required for the bank to commence business was actually paid in by the shareholders. If the bank afterwards failed and the shareholders lost their money, it was not because of the deception practised upon the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's question has no relevancy to the subject now before us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let me read
the motion under discussion:
That this House is of the opinion that a Royal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate the incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada and the granting of the certificate by the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to issue notes and commence business.
The motion is not to examine what took place after the bank had been organized as now suggested, but to examine these circumstances under which the certificate was granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If I understood the motion correctly, it asks for an investigation into the operation and efficiency of the Banking Act in respect of the affairs and transactions of the bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let us read the motion:
That this House is of opinion that a Royal Commission should forthwith issue to inquire into and investigate the incorporation and organization of the Farmers' Bank of Canada, and the granting of a certificate by the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to issue notes and commence business, and all circumstances connected therewith and generally to inquire into and investigate the operation and efficiency of the Bank Act in relation to the affairs and transactions of the said bank.
The fact that the provisions of the Bank Act may be violated is not an argument in favour of the view taken by my hon. friend. We are asked to investigate three things-the incorporation, the organization and the granting of the certificate. As to the granting of the certificate, anything that transpired afterwards, when the bank was in operation, is not relevant to the question.
Will the Prime Minister allow me a question? If the Treasury Board had not given the bank permission to do business, could this loss have occurred?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is very easily answered-certainly not. Had the certificate of the Treasury Board not been granted, the bank could not have begun business; and there would have been no default and no loss. But the object my hon, friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) had in this motion is, after this investigation is granted, the treasury of Canada should come to the rescue of the shareholders. My answer to my hon. friend is there is nologic or relevancy in his question. If the shareholders have lost, the man who was their agent deceived the Treasury Board as well as the shareholders, and the Treasury Board is no more responsible for the laches of the agent of the shareholders than
COMMONo
are the shareholders themselves. I think that is common sense. The government has been deceived by the agent of the shareholders, by the man whom they selected, and in whom they put their confidence. So, I ask my hon. friend himself:	Does he
think that, under such circumstances, it lies in the mouth of the shareholder to tell the government:	You should relieve
us from the effect of the laches of our own agent?

If the hon. gentleman is speaking to me, nay answer is that in the first place the motion does not say anything of the kind, and, in the second place, in the interest of the people, there should be a full investigation so that a disaster like this could not happen again.

May I ask a question? As I understand it, the object of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) is, only if the investigation proves that the issue of the certificate was due to the neglect of the Finance Department, to hold the government_ responsible for protecting the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say that is the object of this motion, as it was plainly stated by my hon. friend from Halton, who spoke, I think, in very clear language. He made it plain that his object was to come to the rescue of the shareholders. He wanted to show that this investigation was only a preliminary step which would ultimately induce parliament to recoup these people for the losses they have suffered. My answer is, simply, if the shareholders have lost, it is because the agent of the shareholders deceived the government as well as the shareholders. And I think it is not a sound principle that anybody should be recouped for a loss made by his own agent.
I dislike to interrupt the Prime Minister, but would he permit me a word?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.

I think you will recollect, Mr. Speaker, that in what I said I divided the question into two parts. I distinctly said that if the loss was all brought about by reason of the action of the men whom the shareholders had put into office, then, they should suffer alone. I was clear on that, I think. But I said that if, on the other hand, the loss was brought about by reason of the action of this government or of the Treasury Board which was part of the government, then I thought this country was big enough, rich enough and generous enough to maintain its own honour and defend these people. That is what I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite willing to discuss the question in the light Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
my friend has placed it, that this country is broad enough, rich enough, to correct an error of the government, if an error has been committed. Undoubtedly the government has been deceived in this matter, but by whom? The government has been deceived by the agent of the very men whom my hon. friend now wants to recoup. The government has been deceived by, Mr. Travers, if by anybody, and Mr. Travers was the agent of the shareholders who had appointed him to his office. Under the circumstances, I think that the suggestion of my hon. friend that the government should come to the rescue of the men who appointed the very man who deceived the government, is a proposition which no one could on reflection be prepared to admit. Now, it has been stated that there is a further question to investigate, the broader question of the sufficiency of the Bank Act. That is a good proposition, and it may be that an investigation might serve a good purpose. But I am not prepared to say at the present time that a case has been made out against the Bank Act; I do not say that later on something may be disclosed of that nature. But I have to observe that at the present time the matter is being investigated^ by the courts, and that there is not sufficient evidence yet disclosed by the courts to show that it is necessary to go further with this investigation. My last word is that at this moment no case has been made out why the motion should be granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to ask the Prime Minister how he can argue that Mr. Travers was the agent of the depositors.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say the depositors. I said the shareholders.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But the depositors are the people who are suffering.
On motion of Mr. Edwards, debate was adjourned.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Lauxier, House adjourned at 12.07 a.m. Thursday.
